## Vision
**juggernaut** is a monorepo that hosts various tools and apps to connect different services and AI agents into one integrated system.
Its core is a **task system**. The distinctive features of juggernaut's task system are:
- A task can be assigned to agents (Claude Cowork, Claude Code, openclaw, codex) so they can poll periodically and pick up tasks to work on via their skills.
- Every AI agent session related to a task is uploaded and attached back to the task for future reference.
juggernaut is a **personal project**, so it does not need to be optimized for throughput (highly scalable) — but it should be **low-latency and delightful**.
juggernaut is **not an AI agent itself**; it is the connecting tissue for third-party AI agents. The monorepo holds skills that agents use to interact with it.

The monorepo also hosts **connectors to data** (bank apps, health apps, etc.) and re-implements some trivial app UIs for better integration (pill tracker, reading tracker, weather app, etc.) based on data available from public open or paid sources.
Additional components juggernaut provides include **web and mobile apps** for management.
## Technical Choices
- **TypeScript** unless something is impossible to implement with TypeScript.

## UI design rule (hard)

**Any user-facing UI change in this repo — new pages, new components, layout or visual tweaks — must go through the `/frontend-design:frontend-design` skill** (already auto-enabled via `.claude/settings.json`). Do not hand-design from scratch. Invoke the skill, review its output, then commit. This applies to `apps/web` and any future `apps/mobile` UI.
## Development procedure
Every change to juggernaut follows these seven steps in order. Do not skip any.

1. **Planning session** — write a plan file under `~/.claude/plans/`. Get user approval before any non-trivial implementation. Reuse `/init`, `/skill-creator`, `/frontend-design` skills where they fit.
2. **Implementation** — make the code changes locally.

3. **Local manual testing** — actually click through the affected UI / `curl` the affected endpoints. Don't rely on type-checking alone. For UI, prefer running `pnpm dev` and using Claude-in-Chrome to verify renders + console-clean.
4. **Run all checks locally** — `pnpm -r run typecheck` + `pnpm --filter @juggernaut/api test`. Per project rule: no CI; everything proven locally first.
5. **Commit and push to remote** — directly on `main` (per project rule: no feature branches).
6. **Wait and verify deployment** — Railway auto-deploys from `main`. Watch the new revision come up healthy in Railway + BetterStack logs.
7. **Manual prod testing** — repeat the relevant happy-path scenarios against the deployed URL. Catches environment-specific issues (env vars, DNS, CORS, Clerk domain config).
## Load-bearing patterns

- **User scoping**: every DB query is scoped by `userId` from the Clerk JWT (`c.var.userId` in Hono). `tasks` and `task_sessions` carry an explicit `user_id` column; children are scoped via FK joins. Never read or write across users.

- **User scoping**: every DB query is scoped by `userId` from the Clerk JWT (`c.var.userId` in Hono). `tasks` and `task_sessions` carry an explicit `user_id` column; children are scoped via FK joins. Never read or write across users. The upload handler (`/api/powersync/upload`) inserts under the JWT's user, whitelists which columns a client may set (never `id`/`user_id`/`task_id`), and scopes every update/delete to the caller — tasks by `user_id` (incl. a `setWhere` on the PUT conflict), child rows by the parent task's owner via an `exists` guard. So an upload can't move a row between users or modify another user's data, even with a forged id.

- **Test auth**: `apps/api/src/app.ts` accepts the auth middleware as a parameter so tests can swap in a stub that reads `x-test-user` instead of verifying a real Clerk JWT. The route handlers themselves never know the difference.

- **PowerSync sync rules** (`apps/powersync/config/sync-config.yaml`): data queries are **single-table — no JOINs** (PowerSync rejects them). Tables with a `user_id` (tasks, task_sessions) use a per-user bucket parameterized by `request.jwt() ->> 'sub'`; child tables (no `user_id`) use a `by_task` bucket whose parameter query lists the user's task ids. `task_session_events` is intentionally **outside** the sync set — fetched on-demand via `GET /api/sessions/:id/events`.

- **PowerSync client isolation**: one local SQLite **file per Clerk user** (`juggernaut-<userId>.db`) so cached rows + the pending upload queue can't leak across accounts (tabs/loads/switches). Dev mode (`VITE_DISABLE_AUTH`) uses a separate `juggernaut-dev.db`. The board/detail queries don't filter by `user_id` — the per-user file + per-user sync buckets are what scope the data.

- **PowerSync upload contract**: jsonb `payload` columns arrive as JSON **strings** (PowerSync stores jsonb as TEXT on the client) — the handler `JSON.parse`s them before Drizzle, and rejects malformed JSON with 400 rather than dropping it. The browser→API call is **cross-origin**, so the API runs `hono/cors` before auth (`WEB_ORIGIN` allowlist); without it the upload preflight 401s and silently never persists.
- **Backend logs**: pino JSON to stdout, never `console.log`. Every state-changing route emits a log line at the end with `event: '<domain>.<action>'` plus relevant IDs.
- **Frontend logs**: import `clientLogger` from `src/lib/clientLogger.ts` — singleton, batches to BetterStack in prod, console-only in dev. Wired to `window.onerror` and `unhandledrejection`.
- **No mocks of internal code**: backend tests run against a real Postgres (PGlite in tests, real Postgres in dev/prod). Only the auth boundary is swapped.
- **No `.js` extensions in workspace package imports**: drizzle-kit's loader can't follow them. Use extensionless imports inside `packages/db-schema/`.

- **Task-comment markdown auto-linkifies** bare `http(s)://…`, URLs wrapped in `**bold**`/`*italic*`, and scheme-less `host.tld/path` (rendered with an `https://` href, displayed as written) — `apps/web/src/routes/task-detail.tsx` (`renderInline`/`renderBody`, shared `INLINE_RE`; the scheme-less match needs a `/path` so prose like `package.json`/`16/9`/`U.S.` isn't mislinked; hrefs forced to http(s)). lines.t: - **Monobank stamps a transfer's two legs to the SAME second, so "the latest transaction" is never `ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 1`.** On a tie Postgres returns an arbitrary row, and for a running-balance read that is a coin flip between the transfer's intermediate and final state. Shipped as a wrong balance: a ФОП account emptied on 2026-08-18 carried two rows both at 21:08:04Z (`+1 575 → 81 112.50`, then `−81 112.50 → 0`) and the app showed 81 113 грн — in the account card AND in the daily net-worth snapshot, which read the same way. The order is recoverable without the timestamps, because a row's OPENING balance is `balance - amount` and the last row's closing balance opens nothing; `latestAccountBalance` (`miniapps/money/src/latest-account-balance.ts`) does that reconstruction and is the ONLY way to read a Monobank account's current balance — use it rather than re-deriving. It returns `no_transactions` / `indeterminate` rather than guessing, and callers keep their previous value; two rules pull opposite ways and are applied at different points, so keep them straight when editing: the scan cap is judged on the RAW row count (dedupe would hide an overflow) while the chain runs on the DEDUPED list (the plun import's twins share ts+amount+balance and would otherwise read as two rival terminal rows and freeze the balance). Read the tied group with `gte(ts, max)`, never `eq` — the driver millisecond-truncates the Date, so `eq` against a finer-precision `ts` matches nothing and freezes the balance silently. **Still open:** `/accounts/balance-history` has no tie-break, so the account page's 180-day chart can still order a tied group arbitrarily.

- **Never use `\b` to whole-word-match a Cyrillic string — use `buildMerchantPattern`.** JS `\b` is a boundary between `\w` (`[A-Za-z0-9_]`) and non-`\w`, and ordinary Cyrillic letters are not `\w` — so at a _normally delimited_ Cyrillic word edge there is no boundary and the match silently fails: `/\bНова пошта\b/.test('Оплата Нова пошта Київ')` is **false** (verified). It is not "never fires" — beside an ASCII word char it does (`'AНова поштаB'` matches), which is exactly why the bug reads as intermittent rather than total. This shipped: `mergeRefundTransactions` added `\b` to stop "WOG" matching "WOGNER", which then broke refund-collapsing for any merchant whose name starts and ends in Cyrillic and sits between ordinary separators — the observed case was «Нова пошта», visible as a charge and its «Скасування.» sitting as two uncollapsed rows (fixed 2026-08-03; the same line still exists in the `legacy/plun` ancestor). The canonical fix already lives in `miniapps/money/src/monobank-client.ts:145` — `buildMerchantPattern` wraps the escaped needle in `(?<![\p{L}\p{N}\p{M}_])…(?![\p{L}\p{N}\p{M}_])` with the `u` flag. Reuse it rather than re-deriving; merchant names, categories and most user-facing strings here are Cyrillic.

- **Calendar days/months are Kyiv-local, never UTC truncation.** Deriving a day string via `toISOString().slice(0, 10)` (or comparing against a `toISOString()` cutoff) files anything that happens between local midnight and the UTC rollover (00:00–03:00 Kyiv) under the wrong date. Use the local-time helpers (`ymd(date)`, the money `useKyivDayKey`/`useKyivMonthKey`) for grouping, display and sorting. This recurred three times in one week (pills "today", money month windows, nanny balance log — the last caught by codex) — treat any new date-keyed feature as suspect until checked. ⚠️ **And a fixed `+3` offset is NOT one of the local-time helpers** — Kyiv is UTC+2 in winter, so swapping a UTC truncation for `ts + 3h` just trades a summer bug for a winter one an hour wide (`2026-12-01T21:30:00Z` is 23:30 on the 1st, which `+3` rolls to the 2nd). Format through `Europe/Kyiv` (`Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-CA', {timeZone:'Europe/Kyiv'})` yields `YYYY-MM-DD`); caught by codex in `miniapps/nanny/src/summary.ts`, where the fixed offset legitimately stays for plun-faithful MONEY boundaries while display days go through the real calendar.

- **Prefer the Drizzle query builder over `db.execute` — the raw-SQL escape hatch returns a DIFFERENT SHAPE in tests than in prod, and both typecheck.** `Database` is typed as `PostgresJsDatabase`, but the test harness passes a `PgliteDatabase`, and their `execute` results disagree: measured 2026-08-24, PGlite returns `{ rows, fields, affectedRows }` and is **not iterable**, while postgres-js returns the row list itself. So `for (const r of await db.execute(...))` or `[...result]` throws `is not iterable` in the suite while being correct in production — or, worse, the reverse for code shaped the other way, which ships a green suite over a broken read. There is currently **no `db.execute` anywhere in `miniapps/` or `apps/api/src`**, and that is worth keeping: `db.select({ ... })` with `sql` expressions for the computed columns (plus `groupBy`) covers the aggregate cases and normalises the result across both drivers. If you genuinely need raw SQL, read `.rows` defensively and test it on BOTH drivers rather than trusting the type.
- **Backend logs**: pino JSON to stdout, never `console.log`. Every state-changing route emits a log line at the end with `event: '<domain>.<action>'` plus relevant IDs.
- **Frontend logs**: import `clientLogger` from `src/lib/clientLogger.ts` — singleton, batches to BetterStack in prod, console-only in dev. Wired to `window.onerror` and `unhandledrejection`.
- **No mocks of internal code**: backend tests run against a real Postgres (PGlite in tests, real Postgres in dev/prod). Only the auth boundary is swapped.
- **No `.js` extensions in workspace package imports**: drizzle-kit's loader can't follow them. Use extensionless imports inside `packages/db-schema/`.

- **Deployed ≠ callable in this process (MCP tool list is process-cached)**: a newly-deployed juggernaut MCP tool can't be called from the long-running Claude Code process that shipped it — the MCP client caches `tools/list` at connect time and doesn't refresh per cron tick (ToolSearch won't find it; existing tools keep their old schemas too). **Reassigning the task to another agent kind does NOT reliably make the tool callable sooner** — observed twice (Jun 2026): after shipping `ask_user`, three consecutive Codex/Cowork runs (incl. a _fresh_ Cowork session 24h later) still couldn't see it — only a full **MCP client reconnect** surfaced it; and the new `vinyl_*` tools stayed invisible to Cowork on reassignment, appearing only ~40 min later while other tools were present. So a new tool can stay invisible to **every** live session — including fresh ones and other agent kinds — for tens of minutes until that client's MCP connection actually reconnects. Practical rule: **don't promise a same-tick dogfood and don't assume "reassign to Cowork" picks it up**; drive the new endpoint via the **REST API** (the reliable fallback) until a session actually surfaces the tool, and only then dogfood the MCP path. Same family as the plugin-version-bump gotcha above ("deployed ≠ visible in this process"), and as the running-vs-installed trap for long-lived local binaries (→ `development-process` step 7).

- **PowerSync local tables can go transiently EMPTY** on the client (a sync reconciliation clears local rows; on mobile the whole local database can disappear between boots). Two corrections measured 2026-08-01/02, both of which had misdirected earlier debugging: the web SDK stores each `dbFilename` as an **IndexedDB** database (the default `IDBBatchAtomicVFS`), **not OPFS** — an OPFS-only inventory looks reassuringly empty and proves nothing; and the loss is **not** a whole-origin eviction — a boot was captured with `localStorage` intact (`freshWebMarker: false`, 241 boots) and zero PowerSync databases on disk, recreated 0.7 s later. So don't infer "storage was evicted" from localStorage state, and don't infer "database is fine" from the marker surviving. For **client-written "sticky" state that doesn't replicate back from Postgres** (read-state, dismissals, local prefs), don't trust the synced table alone — ALSO mirror to `localStorage` and merge latest-wins (this caused the "tasks keep resetting to unread" bug; fixed in `apps/web/src/lib/taskReads.ts`).

- **Prod migrations** run via `pnpm --filter @juggernaut/api migrate:prod drizzle/<file>.sql` — the path is **relative to `apps/api/`, so the `drizzle/` prefix is required**; a bare filename exits `ENOENT` (reads the secret from gitignored `apps/api/.env.prod-migrate.local`; the file's SQL must be visible in the transcript immediately before the run; manual, no migrate-on-boot, backward-compatible by convention). The auto-mode "Production Deploy" classifier auto-approves ONLY additive `ADD COLUMN` (constant DEFAULT) / `CREATE TABLE` / `CREATE INDEX` / a row-scoped backfill `UPDATE`. **`ALTER TYPE … ADD VALUE`** (adding an enum value — common for a new `task_status`/`trigger_kind`) is safe+additive but NOT on the allowlist, so it soft-blocks until the user says "I authorize migration"; DROP/TRUNCATE/DELETE/type-change/column-drop/unbounded-UPDATE are hard-denied. **This hard-deny is route-agnostic: the auto-mode classifier blocks a non-additive prod-DB mutation however you reach it** — a `migrate:prod` DELETE, OR a DELETE issued through a deployed MCP tool / REST endpoint via a direct authenticated `fetch` from the browser (even with the user's own Clerk session token). So _removing_ prod data (e.g. deleting a bad month of rows) can't be done autonomously in auto mode: build + ship the delete capability if it's missing, then hand the actual deletion to the user / an interactive (non-auto) session — don't burn retries trying to route around the guard.

- **Task-comment markdown auto-linkifies** bare `http(s)://…`, URLs wrapped in `**bold**`/`*italic*`, and scheme-less `host.tld/path` (rendered with an `https://` href, displayed as written) — `apps/web/src/routes/task-detail.tsx` (`renderInline`/`renderBody`, shared `INLINE_RE`; the scheme-less match needs a `/path` so prose like `package.json`/`16/9`/`U.S.` isn't mislinked; hrefs forced to http(s)). So agents can post bare/scheme-less URLs in report comments and they stay clickable. Keep the leaf + top-level passes sharing `INLINE_RE` so they don't drift.

- **UI page design bar**: the user values pages that surface _what's happening / what an entity does_ (current work, recent sessions/activity, at-a-glance stat tiles) far above setup/config (demote config to a secondary collapsible). When building/reworking a juggernaut page, lead with informative content from the already-synced client data (tasks by `assignee_id`, `task_sessions` by `created_by_assignee_id`; local SQLite JOINs are fine — don't add endpoints) and rethink the information architecture rather than shuffling existing widgets. All UI still goes through `/frontend-design` + the design-system skill.

there already, reuse it instead of inventing — the "plun file" paths below are repo-relative:

| Concern                      | plun file                                                                                     | how to reuse                                                                                                                         |

| Frontend BetterStack logger  | `legacy/plun/apps/web/packages/frontend/src/utils/clientLogger.ts`                            | Already lifted into `apps/web/src/lib/clientLogger.ts`. Diff against plun's when updating.                                           |

steps.label: PGlite runs every query over ONE serialized connection, so `Promise.all` in a test is INTERLEAVED, not concurrent — a "race" test written that way passes whether or not the locking exists.

lines.t: - **PowerSync web hands out ONE exclusive connection lease per origin AND database file, shared by every tab that opens that database, with a 120 s default lock timeout — so any local read is at the mercy of a tab you are not looking at, and a poller without an in-flight guard makes it worse.** Which primitive enforces it depends on the configuration — desktop multi-tab serialises inside a shared worker, the dedicated-worker fallback takes a navigator lock — so do NOT reason from one of them; the durable fact is the SCOPE: contention needs the origin and the database file to match. Given the per-Clerk-user `juggernaut-<userId>.db` rule below, that means the tabs fighting each other are always the same user's, on the same host. `getUploadQueueStats()` (and anything else taking that lease) waits behind whoever holds it, and the wait is four times longer than the 30 s queue-poll cadence. A `setInterval` that fires regardless therefore stacks waiters behind its own outstanding read, and their failures then arrive together and get counted as independent evidence — measured over 19–24.08 on the desktop watcher: 82 of 958 neighbouring `could not read upload queue stats` rows under two seconds apart, two of them **2 ms** apart from one tab, which one 30 s poller cannot produce. Chrome's background-tab timer throttling is the other half: the median gap between neighbouring failed polls was 60.5 s against a requested 30 s, so **anything computed as `ticks × interval` is fiction — derive durations from clock readings.** The fix pattern is in `apps/web/src/powersync/uploadQueueWatch.ts`: skip the tick while a read is in flight, and declare a detector blind on ELAPSED TIME rather than on a completion count, or the guard silently makes the detector slower and a read that never returns produces no log line at all.

- **Reading the PowerSync reconnect watchdog's logs: `downForMs` is ACCUMULATED downtime, never stall duration — always pair a `reconnect_forced` with the `reconnect_recovered` that follows it before calling anything stuck.** The watchdog (`apps/web/src/powersync/reconnectWatchdog.ts`, component `powersync.watchdog`) stamps `downForMs` with wall-clock time since the connection last went down, which on a backgrounded phone or a slept laptop is mostly time the process wasn't running. Measured 2026-08-21: a `reconnect_forced` carrying `downForMs: 5421890` (**90 min**) and another at **73.7 min** were each followed by `reconnect_recovered` **2 seconds later** — i.e. the watchdog worked perfectly and a `downForMs`-only reading would have reported a 90-minute outage that never happened. Two companion traps in the same rows: `visible: true` does **not** mean a human was looking (macOS sleep never fires `visibilitychange`, so a slept Mac logs `visible: true` throughout), and `reconnect_attempt_error: "Operation aborted by abort controller"` is the watchdog's own 30 s timeout firing, not a network fault. And because `clientLogger` hardcodes `service: 'juggernaut-web'` for the mobile WebView too, **split desktop from mobile by `userAgent`, never by `service`** — in that same window 26 of 27 "visible-tab stalls" were the Android app, not the web app the ticket was about. **Two more splits the same sweep needs.** Frontend custom fields are NESTED: `clientLogger` puts everything a call site passes under a single `context` object (`apps/web/src/lib/clientLogger.ts`), so only `dt`/`level`/`message`/`component`/`userId`/`url`/`userAgent`/`source`/`service` are top-level — a query reading `JSONExtractString(raw,'watchId')` returns an **empty string, not an error**, which reads exactly like a field that was never shipped. Use `JSONExtractString(raw,'context','<field>')`. And the app is served from **two origins** (`plun.me` and `juggernaut.plun.me`, the former carrying most desktop traffic since 21.08), which are two separate local databases — so a desktop sweep must split on the `url` host as well as on `userAgent`.

- **Test auth**: `apps/api/src/app.ts` accepts the auth middleware as a parameter so tests can swap in a stub that reads `x-test-user` instead of verifying a real Clerk JWT. The route handlers themselves never know the difference. **A cross-user isolation test must use ONE harness and the `x-test-user` header — a second `buildHarness()` is a second PGlite instance, i.e. a different database, so "the other user" writes somewhere the assertion can never see.** Such a test does not fail loudly; it passes for the wrong reason. Measured 2026-08-28 on the shopping appliers: two isolation tests failed (the foreign row simply wasn't there to be protected), and a third — "rejects an item filed under another user's group" — went GREEN because the foreign group id matched no row at all, so it proved only that an unknown id is rejected, never that ownership is checked. The tell is an isolation assertion whose setup ran through a harness other than the one under test. Pair every such test with a **positive control** in the same body (the same write against the caller's OWN row must succeed, and the owner's own delete must work), or a 400 that means "always rejected" is indistinguishable from one that means "not yours".

- **PGlite runs every query over ONE serialized connection, so `Promise.all` in a test is INTERLEAVED, not concurrent — a "race" test written that way passes whether or not the locking exists.** The harness (`apps/api/test/harness.ts`) is a single in-process instance; there is no second connection for a second transaction to run in. Measured 2026-08-29 while adding `agent_repo_locks`: a test firing three simultaneous acquires and asserting exactly one wins stayed **green after the `pg_advisory_xact_lock` was deleted from the service** — it had never exercised serialization at all. Two rules follow. **Assert concurrency guarantees where they actually live — in the DATABASE**: a unique index can be tested here (insert the row a losing racer would write, expect the constraint to reject it), and unlike the advisory lock it also fails when you break it. **And prove any guard is load-bearing by REMOVING it and watching the test go red** — for a concurrency test that control is not optional, because passing-for-the-wrong-reason is the default outcome. Where a branch genuinely cannot be reached in PGlite (one transaction observing another's mid-flight insert), say so in the test file rather than writing a test that appears to cover it.

- **PowerSync sync rules** (`apps/powersync/config/sync-config.yaml`): data queries are **single-table — no JOINs** (PowerSync rejects them). There is exactly **ONE** bucket definition, `by_user`, parameterized by `request.jwt() ->> 'sub'`: every synced table carries a `user_id` and filters on `bucket.user_id`. `task_session_events`, `api_tokens`, and `device_auth_requests` are intentionally **outside** the sync set (events fetched on-demand via `GET /api/sessions/:id/events`; the auth tables hold secrets and never reach clients).

- **PowerSync buckets are capped at 1000 per connection, and a parent-id parameter query spends one bucket PER PARENT ROW.** Both `api.parameters.max_buckets_per_connection` and `max_parameter_query_results` default to 1000; crossing that count aborts **every** sync stream instantly (`[PSYNC_S2305]`, `data_sent_bytes: 0`) — a total client freeze on web _and_ mobile while writes keep persisting server-side and the health probes stay green. It reads as a feature bug, not a sync bug (2026-08-05: "a recurring task's next occurrence isn't spawned" — it was; the client never got the row). That outage came from a `by_task` bucket that enumerated the user's task ids; **fixed structurally 2026-08-08** — the seven task child tables now carry their own `user_id`, all live in `by_user`, and `by_task` is deleted, so bucket count no longer tracks task count. The 10000 ceilings in `service.yaml` remain as headroom, not as the mechanism. **So: prefer an owner column over a parent-id parameter query in any NEW bucket definition** — the trap is still live for anyone who adds one. Full symptoms + the six-step rollout an owner column needs on an already-synced table → the repo `railway` skill.

- **PowerSync client isolation**: one local SQLite **file per Clerk user** (`juggernaut-<userId>.db`) so cached rows + the pending upload queue can't leak across accounts (tabs/loads/switches). Dev mode (`VITE_DISABLE_AUTH`) uses a separate `juggernaut-dev.db`. The board/detail queries don't filter by `user_id` — the per-user file + per-user sync buckets are what scope the data.

- **PowerSync upload contract**: jsonb `payload` columns arrive as JSON **strings** (PowerSync stores jsonb as TEXT on the client) — the handler `JSON.parse`s them before Drizzle, and rejects malformed JSON with 400 rather than dropping it. The browser→API call is **cross-origin**, so the API runs `hono/cors` before auth (`WEB_ORIGIN` allowlist); without it the upload preflight 401s and silently never persists.

- **Validate constraint-bound columns in the client BEFORE a local-first `db.execute` — the optimistic write is not the safety net, the upload is.** A value that violates a Postgres constraint (a decimal into an `integer` column, an out-of-enum string, a NOT-NULL left null, a value the applier 400s) writes fine to the local SQLite and renders optimistically, then **fails the PowerSync upload and WEDGES the whole upload queue** — every later write stalls behind the poison entry, silently. So the web write path must mirror the server applier's checks (type/range/enum/not-null) before `db.execute`, and a fresh singleton row must seed its NOT-NULL columns. Bit us on books `total_pages`/`current_page` (decimals) and the newborn benefits/config seed (`vitamin_d_enabled`); both caught by codex/pre-empted. This is the client-side twin of the applier validation — a bad value never reaching the queue is the only reliable guard.

- **Every synced table the client WRITES to needs a case in the upload applier — a missing one wedges that device's entire queue, not just that table.** The bullet above is about a bad VALUE; this is the same wedge reached by a table the applier simply doesn't know, which falls through to the default `unsupported table` 400. One batch is one server transaction, so the poison entry takes its innocent batch-mates down with it and PowerSync retries the pair forever. Diagnosed 2026-08-10: deleting a comment that had a file attached uploads `{comment_attachments: 1, task_comments: 1}` (`deleteComment` clears both tables in one local transaction), `comment_attachments` had no applier case, and the phone uploaded **nothing** for the next four hours — 167 identical failures, `applied=0` every time. **The signature is the giveaway, because it looks nothing like a sync bug**: reads keep flowing, the app looks connected, the sync service is green, and the only tell is the client's **write checkpoint frozen at one number while the read checkpoint climbs** (`Updated checkpoint: <read> | write: <frozen>` in the `juggernaut-powersync` Railway logs, one line per client). The audit is mechanical, and **`apps/api/test/powersync-applier-coverage.test.ts` now runs it for you** — it diffs the `case '<table>':` labels in `routes/powersync.ts` against every table `apps/web/src`/`apps/mobile/src` runs an INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on, in both directions, so a new synced table that the client writes and the applier doesn't know fails the suite instead of the phone. Its ONE exemption is `apps/mobile/src/visualTest.ts` (build-flag-gated, separate DB); if you add another, prove it cannot reach a real upload queue. Where the client's write is a mirror of an authoritative REST call, the applier case should **acknowledge and do nothing** rather than repeat the mutation: a second destructive path keyed only on a row id is what a replayed queue entry turns into a data-loss bug. **The wedge is now also VISIBLE**: `apps/web/src/powersync/uploadQueueHealth.ts` counts consecutive upload failures and watches the pending queue, and `UploadQueueAlert` in `components/shell-shared.tsx` puts a red strip under the header of both shells (plus a fourth `SyncStatusPill` state) — the pill's other three states are all download signals, which is why it read СИНХРОНІЗОВАНО throughout the four-hour outage.

- **Three schemas stay in lockstep — adding a column to a synced table is a 3-file change.** A PowerSync-synced table is defined in THREE places that must agree: the Drizzle table (`packages/db-schema/`), the prod Postgres (a migration), and the **web client schema** (`apps/web/src/powersync/schema.ts`). The sync rules `SELECT *` every synced table, so **a column added to the DB but missing from the client schema wedges an already-synced client's incremental sync** — the whole board silently freezes (task state, comments, sessions stop updating on the UI even though writes persist server-side; a _fresh_ client looks fine, which makes it easy to miss). This bit us once (`recurrence_assignee_id` on task_recurrence). When you add/rename/drop a column on a synced table, update all three. `apps/api/test/powersync-schema-sync.test.ts` enforces it — it parses the sync rules + Drizzle columns + the web schema and fails if a `SELECT *` table's client schema is missing a column. **Explicit-column tables have a fourth contract:** every column used by the sync rule, including an owner used only in `WHERE`, must also be in the Postgres publication projection. `comment_attachments` omitted `user_id` there and silently vanished from every by_user bucket while REST kept working (fixed by 0093; guarded by the same test). Its curated client projection may still omit server-only columns. **A whole NEW synced table is another publication step**: prod uses an explicit table list (not `FOR ALL TABLES`), so add it via an `ALTER PUBLICATION` migration, and row-touch anything written before membership or projection was correct — full pattern + symptoms in the repo `railway` skill. **And warn the user BEFORE you ship it: any sync-rules change invalidates every bucket, so every client re-downloads its ENTIRE bucket once** (`reason="checkpoint_superseded"`). Measured 2026-08-12 adding `media_duel`: the phone pulled **38 335 operations / 51 MB over ~7 minutes**, during which the sync pill honestly showed the LAST COMPLETED sync — a timestamp frozen ~30 min in the past — and read exactly like a sync outage. Nothing is broken and it self-heals; the cost is the surprise. Say it in the report, and expect a stale pill for minutes after any sync-rules deploy.

- **Clearing a field on a recurrence BLUEPRINT is not done until every OCCURRENCE row is cleared too — otherwise the next schedule edit silently puts it back.** `applyRecurrenceUpload` (`apps/api/src/routes/powersync.ts`) computes `recValues.brief = hasBrief ? resolved.brief : (existingRecurrence?.brief ?? null)` — and the same line for `skill` — then feeds that straight into `blueprintSet`. A PATCH carries only the columns that changed, so **any ordinary schedule edit in the web UI reads the OCCURRENCE's stored value and writes it back onto the blueprint**. Measured 2026-08-26 while emptying the `brief` column: 103 `task_recurrence` rows still held text, and three of those texts belonged to blueprints that migrations `0119`/`0120` had cleaned weeks earlier — all of them one schedule tap away from resurrection. So a data migration that nulls a blueprint field must null the mirrors in the same transaction (0117, 0119, 0120, 0122 and 0128 all do), and a cleanup that touches only `task_recurrence_blueprints` is not a smaller version of the change — it is a change that undoes itself. The trap outlives `brief`: `skill` travels the identical path.

- **`money_transactions`' `amount` is in the OPERATION currency, `balanceAfter` in the ACCOUNT's — never do arithmetic across the two without checking `currencyCode`.** The MCP tool says so, and it is still easy to miss because both render as plain numbers. Cost a wrong published diagnosis on 2026-08-19: the ФОП account's incoming leg reads `amount: 1575, currencyCode: 978, balanceAfter: 81112.5` — 1575 **EUR**, 81 112.50 **UAH** — and reasoning `81112.5 - 1575` produced a confident, wrong chain. The raw `money_monobank_transaction.amount` column IS in account currency (there: `+8_111_250` kopiykas), which is why the code was right while the human-facing explanation was not. **When a row's `currencyCode` differs from its account's currency, the only figure you may combine with `balance` is the raw column, never the tool's `amount`.**

- **A Monobank row's RAW `amount` and RAW `currencyCode` can name DIFFERENT currencies, and on a cross-currency operation they do — so `convertToUah(tx.amount, tx.currencyCode, rates)` over a Monobank row is only correct while the two happen to agree.** The bullet above records that `money_monobank_transaction.amount` is in the **account's** currency; the other half is that `money_monobank_transaction.currencyCode` is the **operation's**. Both legs of the 2026-08-19 ФОП payout show it: the ФОП **euro** account's leg is `amount −157_500` (−1 575.00 **EUR**, the account) with `currencyCode 980` (**UAH**, the operation), and the ФОП **hryvnia** account's leg is `amount +8_111_250` (81 112.50 **UAH**) with `currencyCode 978` (**EUR**). Because a same-currency operation is the overwhelming normal case, anything built on "currencyCode describes amount" looks correct for months and then silently mis-scales one row by the FX rate. `income-rollup.ts` did exactly this pairing until 2026-08-28 and now resolves the account's currency through `MonobankAccountInfo.currencyCode`; the trap itself is live for any NEW code, so resolve the ACCOUNT's currency through `accountId` in `moneyAccount` whenever the two may differ. ⚠️ And note `money_account.currency` is a **text** column that may hold `'EUR'` as easily as `'978'` — a bare `Number()` yields NaN, which compares equal to nothing (so a same-currency pair reads as cross-currency) and matches no rate series, so the failure is a silently dropped figure rather than an error. Use `toCurrencyCode`.

- **A transfer's two legs are valued at the transfer day's own NBU rate, and their hryvnia difference is a FEE — never income.** Shipped 2026-08-28 (`633d229`) to Yarik's rule: negative difference → an expense in `finance`, positive → a return that subtracts from it. The one implementation is `computeTransferFeeUah` (`miniapps/money/src/transfer-fx.ts`); the spend rollup books it for Monobank **and** manual pairs, and `withVirtualTransferFees` emits the matching ledger row, so the bar and its drilldown agree. Two rules inside it are load-bearing and were each proven by deleting them: a CROSS-currency pair with no same-day rate returns **null and books nothing** (its delta is what survives subtracting two large converted numbers, so any other day's rate is noise the size of the answer), while a SAME-currency delta may fall back to today's rates (a few units of one currency, which an off-day rate can only mis-scale slightly). The day key is **Kyiv, not UTC** — the 19.08.2026 payout is 21:08Z on the 18th, and the wrong day moves a 520 ₴ answer by 35 ₴. What this replaced: the Monobank branch subtracted the legs' RAW amounts without comparing currencies and booked any positive result as «Курсова різниця» income, which on that payout was `81 112,50 ₴ − 1 575,00 € = 79 537,50` — 18% of August 2026's reported income, from money that was never income. **August now reads 371 213,63 ₴ against 450 755 ₴ before, verified on prod.** ⚠️ **These conversions are ROUTINE, not a one-off**: the 2026-08-25 session concluded from a description-text search that the 19.08 transfer was the only one in the history, and the shipped rollup immediately found spreads in June, July and August (−592,12 ₴ in August alone). So `for (const r of await db.execute(...))` or `[...result]` throws `is not iterable` in the suite while being correct in production — or, worse, the reverse for code shaped the other way, which ships a green suite over a broken read. lines.t: - **PowerSync upload contract**: jsonb `payload` columns arrive as JSON **strings** (PowerSync stores jsonb as TEXT on the client) — the handler `JSON.parse`s them before Drizzle, and rejects malformed JSON with 400 rather than dropping it. The browser→API call is **cross-origin**, so the API runs `hono/cors` before auth (`WEB_ORIGIN` allowlist); without it the upload preflight 401s and silently never persists.

- **Validate constraint-bound columns in the client BEFORE a local-first `db.execute` — the optimistic write is not the safety net, the upload is.** A value that violates a Postgres constraint (a decimal into an `integer` column, an out-of-enum string, a NOT-NULL left null, a value the applier 400s) writes fine to the local SQLite and renders optimistically, then **fails the PowerSync upload and WEDGES the whole upload queue** — every later write stalls behind the poison entry, silently. So the web write path must mirror the server applier's checks (type/range/enum/not-null) before `db.execute`, and a fresh singleton row must seed its NOT-NULL columns. Bit us on books `total_pages`/`current_page` (decimals) and the newborn benefits/config seed (`vitamin_d_enabled`); both caught by codex/pre-empted. This is the client-side twin of the applier validation — a bad value never reaching the queue is the only reliable guard.

- **Every synced table the client WRITES to needs a case in the upload applier — a missing one wedges that device's entire queue, not just that table.** The bullet above is about a bad VALUE; this is the same wedge reached by a table the applier simply doesn't know, which falls through to the default `unsupported table` 400. One batch is one server transaction, so the poison entry takes its innocent batch-mates down with it and PowerSync retries the pair forever. Diagnosed 2026-08-10: deleting a comment that had a file attached uploads `{comment_attachments: 1, task_comments: 1}` (`deleteComment` clears both tables in one local transaction), `comment_attachments` had no applier case, and the phone uploaded **nothing** for the next four hours — 167 identical failures, `applied=0` every time. **The signature is the giveaway, because it looks nothing like a sync bug**: reads keep flowing, the app looks connected, the sync service is green, and the only tell is the client's **write checkpoint frozen at one number while the read checkpoint climbs** (`Updated checkpoint: <read> | write: <frozen>` in the `juggernaut-powersync` Railway logs, one line per client). The audit is mechanical, and **`apps/api/test/powersync-applier-coverage.test.ts` now runs it for you** — it diffs the `case '<table>':` labels in `routes/powersync.ts` against every table `apps/web/src`/`apps/mobile/src` runs an INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on, in both directions, so a new synced table that the client writes and the applier doesn't know fails the suite instead of the phone. Its ONE exemption is `apps/mobile/src/visualTest.ts` (build-flag-gated, separate DB); if you add another, prove it cannot reach a real upload queue. Where the client's write is a mirror of an authoritative REST call, the applier case should **acknowledge and do nothing** rather than repeat the mutation: a second destructive path keyed only on a row id is what a replayed queue entry turns into a data-loss bug. **The wedge is now also VISIBLE**: `apps/web/src/powersync/uploadQueueHealth.ts` counts consecutive upload failures and watches the pending queue, and `UploadQueueAlert` in `components/shell-shared.tsx` puts a red strip under the header of both shells (plus a fourth `SyncStatusPill` state) — the pill's other three states are all download signals, which is why it read СИНХРОНІЗОВАНО throughout the four-hour outage.

- **A column on a `SELECT *` synced table cannot be shipped by an UNATTENDED run — the precondition is unverifiable at night, so design around it instead of waiting.** The bullet below makes the client schema declare a new column before the migration adds it; the note on `pills.profile_id` adds that the declaration must also have reached the PHONE via a Capgo OTA first, because `apps/mobile` bundles the same schema file and cannot learn it from a git push. **What nobody wrote down is that a night run cannot CHECK that.** The only signal for which bundle the phone holds is the `build_info` row it logs at boot, and BetterStack's SQL-queryable retention is **~1 hour** (measured 2026-09-01: `min(dt)` 02:50Z, `max(dt)` 03:50Z) — so a phone that has not been woken inside that hour simply cannot be asked, and no amount of waiting helps at 04:00. The honest options are therefore two, and "apply it anyway" is not one: split the increment across two runs the way `pills.profile_id` was, or **pick a shape that touches no synced table at all**. Increment 5 of the medical miniapp took the second: its provenance ledger `medical_extraction` (migration 0141) is server-only — absent from the sync rules, the publication and the client schema, the same treatment as `medical_visit_document_blob` — which invalidates no bucket, needs no OTA, and shipped in one run. Reach for that whenever the new data has no client reader yet.

Both were caught in review on `medical_extraction`, which now carries no FK at all on `document_id`, `pill_id` or `newborn_event_id` — matching `pill_intakes.pill_id` and `medical_visit.profile_id`, and keeping rollback working after the source is deleted. The general rule: **anything the applier can delete must not be the target of a constraint that can fail.**

The sync rules `SELECT *` every synced table, so **a column added to the DB but missing from the client schema wedges an already-synced client's incremental sync** — the whole board silently freezes (task state, comments, sessions stop updating on the UI even though writes persist server-side; a _fresh_ client looks fine, which makes it easy to miss). This bit us once (`recurrence_assignee_id` on task_recurrence). Match in the same encoding (`json.dumps(s, ensure_ascii=True)[1:-1]`) and **assert the occurrence count before writing**, or re-serialise the parsed JSON. Measured 2026-08-31 adding the `silpo` skill, where an assert caught it; without one the run would have reported a description update that never happened.

- **Calendar days/months are Kyiv-local, never UTC truncation.** Deriving a day string via `toISOString().slice(0, 10)` (or comparing against a `toISOString()` cutoff) files anything that happens between local midnight and the UTC rollover (00:00–03:00 Kyiv) under the wrong date. Use the local-time helpers (`ymd(date)`, the money `useKyivDayKey`/`useKyivMonthKey`) for grouping, display and sorting. This recurred three times in one week (pills "today", money month windows, nanny balance log — the last caught by codex) — treat any new date-keyed feature as suspect until checked. ⚠️ **And a fixed `+3` offset is NOT one of the local-time helpers** — Kyiv is UTC+2 in winter, so swapping a UTC truncation for `ts + 3h` just trades a summer bug for a winter one an hour wide (`2026-12-01T21:30:00Z` is 23:30 on the 1st, which `+3` rolls to the 2nd). Format through `Europe/Kyiv` (`Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-CA', {timeZone:'Europe/Kyiv'})` yields `YYYY-MM-DD`); caught by codex in `miniapps/nanny/src/summary.ts`, where the fixed offset legitimately stays for plun-faithful MONEY boundaries while display days go through the real calendar.

- **Prefer the Drizzle query builder over `db.execute` — the raw-SQL escape hatch returns a DIFFERENT SHAPE in tests than in prod, and both typecheck.** `Database` is typed as `PostgresJsDatabase`, but the test harness passes a `PgliteDatabase`, and their `execute` results disagree: measured 2026-08-24, PGlite returns `{ rows, fields, affectedRows }` and is **not iterable**, while postgres-js returns the row list itself. So `for (const r of await db.execute(...))` or `[...result]` throws `is not iterable` in the suite while being correct in production — or, worse, the reverse for code shaped the other way, which ships a green suite over a broken read. There is currently **no `db.execute` anywhere in `miniapps/` or `apps/api/src`**, and that is worth keeping: `db.select({ ... })` with `sql` expressions for the computed columns (plus `groupBy`) covers the aggregate cases and normalises the result across both drivers. If you genuinely need raw SQL, read `.rows` defensively and test it on BOTH drivers rather than trusting the type.

- **Never interpolate a JS `Date` (or any non-primitive) into a raw `` sql`` `` template — encode it first. This is the same PGlite-vs-postgres-js split as the bullet above, one level down, and it is worse because the suite is structurally incapable of catching it.** Drizzle encodes a value only when it knows the COLUMN; inside a `` sql`` `` template it binds with the **noop encoder**, so the value reaches the driver exactly as written. postgres.js then throws `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE … Received an instance of Date`, while **PGlite accepts the raw Date and the test passes**. Measured 2026-08-24: the music library-pass job failed on **every tick from the moment the miniapp shipped** (100 %, zero pages persisted) because its re-like guard interpolated `${track.addedAt}` — and the column-typed `addedAt` two lines above, same value, was encoded to an ISO string and worked. Two `library pass` tests exercise that exact statement and stayed green the whole time. So: write `${d.toISOString()}` (the repo's other two Date-derived interpolations already do), and where a raw template is unavoidable on a hot path, **test it by compiling the statement on the PRODUCTION dialect and asserting on `toSQL().params`** — `apps/api/test/music-collector-params.test.ts` is the worked pattern: it needs no database, is blind to the driver split, and goes red on the unencoded version. The general rule this is the second instance of: **a green suite proves nothing about a code path whose behaviour differs between the test driver and the prod driver — the assertion has to move to something both share**, which here is the compiled query.

- **A fixture SMALL enough to be readable can make a scale-dependent policy look correct — when the code embodies a POLICY whose payoff is emergent, measure the outcome over a simulated run, then re-measure with the mechanism removed.** Sibling of the two driver-split rules above, one axis over: there the suite and prod disagree about the DRIVER, here about the SIZE. Measured 2026-08-27 on the music duel's pair picker. Its job is to make a top-30 reachable out of 5 356 tracks in a few hundred answers; it always opened a question with a never-dealt track, matched against the placed track nearest its strength. Every unit test passed, and so did a 40-item simulation — because in a 40-item pool the supply of fresh tracks RUNS OUT, after which placed tracks start meeting each other. At real scale it never runs out: side A is permanently at strength 0, its opponent is permanently "whoever is nearest 0", and a track that wins twice moves away from 0 and is **never asked about again** — dying one duel short of the three a placement needs. Caught only by `codex review` reasoning about the real pool size, then confirmed by re-running the 300-item simulation, where the true best track finished **second** behind a middling anchor. The fix (alternate a coverage round with a promotion round) is pinned by a test that asserts an OUTCOME — a full top-30 after 100 answers, and the true top-5 in order — and goes red when the promotion round is disabled. **So: for a heuristic, "the tests pass" is not evidence; the assertion has to be a measured outcome at a realistic size, with a control run that has the mechanism switched off.**

- **Never build an error message from `String(err)` on a spawned child — Node puts the FULL argv in it, so anything secret in the argv is now in your logs.** `execFile`'s rejection message is `Command failed: <cmd> <argv joined>` (verified 2026-08-26), and `apps/cli` spawns herdr with `--env JUGGERNAUT_CLAUDE_TOKEN=jg_…` — so the obvious `catch (err) { message: String(err) }` writes a live roster key onto the `juggernaut start` panel and into `juggernaut start > log.txt`. It reads as harmless boilerplate, which is why it survived review twice. The fix belongs at the ONE place the message is built, not at each call site that renders it: `herdr()` in `apps/cli/src/herdr.ts` now returns `herdrCommandLabel(args)` (subcommand only, stops at the first flag) and `herdr.test.ts` drives a real failing call to assert the token is absent. Same rule for any future child process carrying a credential in its arguments — and prefer passing the secret via `env` where the API allows, since an argv is also visible in `ps`.

- **Code shared between `apps/web` and the server lives in `@juggernaut/platform` behind a SUBPATH export, never the package index.** The index pulls in hono, drizzle and pino, which have no business in a browser bundle — so `packages/platform/src/duel-fit.ts` is exported as `@juggernaut/platform/duel-fit` and imported by that path from both sides. The rule exists because the alternative is worse than it looks: the duel RATING is the same Bradley–Terry fit for /books, /movies, the /music page and the top-100 playlist job, and the second implementation that "temporarily" appeared on the server came with a test asserting the two agreed — a duplication with a guard bolted on, which `tsc` correctly refused (a backend test cannot import from `apps/web`: `rootDir`). If a shared thing needs a server-only dependency it does not belong in a subpath module at all.
- **Backend logs**: pino JSON to stdout, never `console.log`. Every state-changing route emits a log line at the end with `event: '<domain>.<action>'` plus relevant IDs.

- **A thrown `HTTPException` NEVER reaches an outer middleware's `catch` — Hono converts it to a response at the dispatch level of the handler that threw, so every handled 4xx used to be invisible by construction.** `compose()` (hono/dist/compose.js) wraps EACH middleware level in its own try/catch and calls `onError` there, sets `context.res`, and returns normally — so `logMiddleware`'s `await next()` never throws and the request records only `request.end status:400`, with no reason anywhere. `app.onError` returned the response without logging, so this was true of the WHOLE API, not one route. It cost 11 days on four paired 400s (task `5d7f6a24`) whose diagnosis was blocked on exactly this. `app.onError` now emits one `request.rejected` line (`apps/api/src/app.ts`); **`onError` is the only place a handled error object still exists, so any future per-status diagnostics belong there, not in the log middleware.** Pinned by `apps/api/test/request-rejected-logging.test.ts`, which goes red if the call is removed.

lines.t: - **User scoping**: every DB query is scoped by `userId` from the Clerk JWT or API token (`c.var.userId` in Hono). `tasks`, `task_sessions`, `assignees`, `api_tokens` carry an explicit `user_id` column; children are scoped via FK joins. Never read or write across users. The upload handler (`/api/powersync/upload`) inserts under the caller's user, whitelists which columns a client may set (never `id`/`user_id`/`task_id`), and scopes every update/delete to the caller — tasks by `user_id` (incl. a `setWhere` on the PUT conflict), child rows by the parent task's owner via an `exists` guard. Cross-table references are ownership-checked too: a task's `assignee_id` (REST or upload) must point at one of the caller's own `assignees` rows.

- **Batch upserts: collapse duplicate keys BEFORE the insert, and report the two kinds of duplicate separately.** Postgres `ON CONFLICT` cannot see a conflict *inside its own statement* — two rows carrying the same key in one `VALUES` list raise `21000` rather than being arbitrated — so any tool taking an array (`shopping_suggest` is the first) must de-duplicate on the way in. The subtler half, caught by its own test on 03.09.2026: an entry collapsed intra-batch shares its key with the sibling row that *was* created, so computing "what failed" as `input.filter(v => !createdKeys.has(v.key))` marks it **successful** and it vanishes silently. Track the intra-batch collapses separately and concatenate. `miniapps/shopping/src/mcp-silpo.ts`.

- **Reading a repo lock — "free" must be a POSITIVE answer, never the absence of one.** `GET /api/repo-locks` (or `list_git_locks`) is the only way to know whether another agent holds a working tree, and the obvious wait loop — grep the response for your path, treat "no match" as free — reports FREE on an empty body, a 502, or a dropped connection. Measured 2026-09-07: one blipped curl inside a poll declared the tree free while a night session was still writing in it, and the "wait" that produced it had been running correctly for the previous 45 minutes. Check the HTTP status is 200 and parse the JSON before believing either answer; on anything else the honest verdict is "I don't know", which is a different thing from "free". The same rule applies to the lock ITSELF: an agent that cannot take one (a day pane before `start_pair_session` existed, a human at the keyboard) is invisible to the protocol, so a clean `locks: []` means "nobody who asks is holding it", not "nobody is editing it".

- **Agent permission model**: API-token actors (`c.var.actor != null`) may only set task status `todo/in_progress/paused/blocked/plan_review` and reassign — `done`/`cancelled`, priority, title and `completedAt` are **human-only** (`assertAgentTaskUpdateAllowed` in `services/tasks.ts`; the PowerSync upload rejects agent tokens outright). Agents propose those via `task_suggestions` (REST `POST /api/tasks/:id/suggestions`, MCP `suggest_change`); resolution (`POST /api/suggestions/:id/resolve`) is human-only and applies the change with actor null in one tx. `completedAt` is stamped server-side on the done transition (REST + upload paths) — clients never send it. **Plan-review loop**: an agent submits a plan by posting it (session summary/comment) and setting `plan_review` + `@me`; the task page's review panel approves or rejects-with-feedback via local-first writes that return the task to `todo` + the plan author (`nextTask` only serves `todo`, so `plan_review` parks tasks out of agent queues).

- **Assignee registry**: tasks reference `assignees` (per-user roster) via `tasks.assignee_id` — no assignee enum on tasks. Every user has an undeletable `@me` row (kind `human`), **lazily upserted** by `ensureSelfAssignee` (assignees list, task create, upload default). Deleting an assignee reassigns their tasks to `@me` **and revokes its bound token**. Cosmetic identity (`display_name`, `avatar` — a ≤96KB data-URL set via `PUT /api/assignees/:id/avatar`) is agent-self-editable (own row only); the canonical `name` is human-only. Assignee writes are **API-only**; PowerSync syncs the table down read-only. Agent roster names can never collide with human rows (`ensureAgentAssignee` refuses, incl. `@me`).

- **Malformed uuid path params are screened per-resolver, at exactly the point the route already resolves a valid-but-unknown id.** `isUuid` (`apps/api/src/uuid.ts`) guards a resolver so a malformed id 404s instead of reaching Postgres and 500ing on `invalid input syntax for type uuid`. **Coverage is per-resolver and NOT complete** — the tasks/sessions/questions/suggestions/assignees/oauth/token resolvers are screened, but `apps/api/test/malformed-uuid-params.test.ts` only exercises the **task-id, session-id and assignee-id** families — a regression in the question-answer, suggestion-resolve, OAuth-client or token-revoke guards would keep the suite green. The subscription usage routes (`POST /:id/usage`, `GET /:id/usage/history`, `/usage/series`) still pass the raw param into `eq(subscriptions.id, …)` and therefore still 500. Screen them when you next touch them; don't assume a route is covered because this rule exists. **The invariant is equivalence, not a fixed position in the handler**: a malformed id and a **valid-but-unknown** uuid must return the SAME status (`apps/api/test/malformed-uuid-params.test.ts`) — which is also what stops a "fixed" 404 from being a coincidence. So place the check immediately before the first SQL use of that id and let it inherit whatever precedence the route already has: on body-bearing routes that call `ensureTaskOwned` first (comments, sessions) an unknown task 404s before the body is ever parsed, so the screen belongs there too, ahead of the payload check. The failure mode is moving it EARLIER than that point: hoisted above an ownership/permission check it turns 403 into 404; hoisted above a body parse on a route that validates the body first it turns 400 into 404. Screening where the resolver actually consumes the id is what keeps both contracts intact.

- **PowerSync web hands out ONE exclusive connection lease per origin AND database file, shared by every tab that opens that database, with a 120 s default lock timeout — so any local read is at the mercy of a tab you are not looking at, and a poller without an in-flight guard makes it worse.** Which primitive enforces it depends on the configuration — desktop multi-tab serialises inside a shared worker, the dedicated-worker fallback takes a navigator lock — so do NOT reason from one of them; the durable fact is the SCOPE: contention needs the origin and the database file to match. Given the per-Clerk-user `juggernaut-<userId>.db` rule below, that means the tabs fighting each other are always the same user's, on the same host. `getUploadQueueStats()` (and anything else taking that lease) waits behind whoever holds it, and the wait is four times longer than the 30 s queue-poll cadence. A `setInterval` that fires regardless therefore stacks waiters behind its own outstanding read, and their failures then arrive together and get counted as independent evidence — measured over 19–24.08 on the desktop watcher: 82 of 958 neighbouring `could not read upload queue stats` rows under two seconds apart, two of them **2 ms** apart from one tab, which one 30 s poller cannot produce. Chrome's background-tab timer throttling is the other half: the median gap between neighbouring failed polls was 60.5 s against a requested 30 s, so **anything computed as `ticks × interval` is fiction — derive durations from clock readings.** The fix pattern is in `apps/web/src/powersync/uploadQueueWatch.ts`: skip the tick while a read is in flight, and declare a detector blind on ELAPSED TIME rather than on a completion count, or the guard silently makes the detector slower and a read that never returns produces no log line at all.

- **Reading an upload-queue blind report: `skippedTicks` is the tab's LIVENESS PROOF, no field names the lease HOLDER, and a quiet window after a tab RELOAD is not evidence that anything was fixed.** `beginTick` (`apps/web/src/powersync/uploadQueueWatch.ts`) increments `skippedTicks` only when the poll timer actually fires with a read still outstanding, so `skippedTicks: 3` on a `queue_watch_blind` means the tab ran three times *during its own blind window* — a frozen tab or a slept Mac cannot produce it, which makes it the positive liveness signal `visible` cannot give (per the bullet above, macOS sleep never fires `visibilitychange`). Measured 2026-08-28 07:37Z, the only blind episode in the 74 h after `ded2be2`: two desktop tabs on `juggernaut.plun.me`, both `reason: no_answer`, `consecutive: 0`, `err: null`, `skippedTicks: 3`, `inFlightForMs` 90 003 and 119 989 — both awake and ticking while their reads went unanswered, the second right up to the SDK's 120 s lock timeout, i.e. the same wait that used to surface as `TimeoutError: signal timed out`. **So a blind report describes the WAITER and only the waiter.** Its `url` says nothing about who holds the lease — at that moment the same origin+database also carried a backgrounded `/money/income` tab armed six hours earlier — so "the blind tab was on /agents" does NOT clear the money routes; naming the holder needs instrumentation on the HOLDING side, which the waiter-side fields structurally cannot supply. And before crediting any fix here, check for a reload: the symptom's 2026-08-25 20:11:58Z stop was one (last warn 20:11:58, `queue_watch_sighted` 20:12:21, fresh `queue_watch_armed` 20:12:55) — a full day BEFORE the fix deployed, because the symptom lives in a tab's AGE and reloading resets it. Normalise any before/after count by desktop `queue_watch_armed` per day, or a quiet week merely means the browser was not left open.

- **Reading the PowerSync reconnect watchdog's logs: `downForMs` is ACCUMULATED downtime, never stall duration — always pair a `reconnect_forced` with the `reconnect_recovered` that follows it before calling anything stuck.** The watchdog (`apps/web/src/powersync/reconnectWatchdog.ts`, component `powersync.watchdog`) stamps `downForMs` with wall-clock time since the connection last went down, which on a backgrounded phone or a slept laptop is mostly time the process wasn't running. Measured 2026-08-21: a `reconnect_forced` carrying `downForMs: 5421890` (**90 min**) and another at **73.7 min** were each followed by `reconnect_recovered` **2 seconds later** — i.e. the watchdog worked perfectly and a `downForMs`-only reading would have reported a 90-minute outage that never happened. Two companion traps in the same rows: `visible: true` does **not** mean a human was looking (macOS sleep never fires `visibilitychange`, so a slept Mac logs `visible: true` throughout), and `reconnect_attempt_error: "Operation aborted by abort controller"` is the watchdog's own 30 s timeout firing, not a network fault. And because `clientLogger` hardcodes `service: 'juggernaut-web'` for the mobile WebView too, **split desktop from mobile by `userAgent`, never by `service`** — in that same window 26 of 27 "visible-tab stalls" were the Android app, not the web app the ticket was about. **Two more splits the same sweep needs.** Frontend custom fields are NESTED: `clientLogger` puts everything a call site passes under a single `context` object (`apps/web/src/lib/clientLogger.ts`), so only `dt`/`level`/`message`/`component`/`userId`/`url`/`userAgent`/`source`/`service` are top-level — a query reading `JSONExtractString(raw,'watchId')` returns an **empty string, not an error**, which reads exactly like a field that was never shipped. Use `JSONExtractString(raw,'context','<field>')`. And the app is served from **two origins** (`plun.me` and `juggernaut.plun.me`, the former carrying most desktop traffic since 21.08), which are two separate local databases — so a desktop sweep must split on the `url` host as well as on `userAgent`.

- **Test auth**: `apps/api/src/app.ts` accepts the auth middleware as a parameter so tests can swap in a stub that reads `x-test-user` instead of verifying a real Clerk JWT. The route handlers themselves never know the difference. **A cross-user isolation test must use ONE harness and the `x-test-user` header — a second `buildHarness()` is a second PGlite instance, i.e. a different database, so "the other user" writes somewhere the assertion can never see.** Such a test does not fail loudly; it passes for the wrong reason. Measured 2026-08-28 on the shopping appliers: two isolation tests failed (the foreign row simply wasn't there to be protected), and a third — "rejects an item filed under another user's group" — went GREEN because the foreign group id matched no row at all, so it proved only that an unknown id is rejected, never that ownership is checked. The tell is an isolation assertion whose setup ran through a harness other than the one under test. Pair every such test with a **positive control** in the same body (the same write against the caller's OWN row must succeed, and the owner's own delete must work), or a 400 that means "always rejected" is indistinguishable from one that means "not yours".

- **PGlite runs every query over ONE serialized connection, so `Promise.all` in a test is INTERLEAVED, not concurrent — a "race" test written that way passes whether or not the locking exists.** The harness (`apps/api/test/harness.ts`) is a single in-process instance; there is no second connection for a second transaction to run in. Measured 2026-08-29 while adding `agent_repo_locks`: a test firing three simultaneous acquires and asserting exactly one wins stayed **green after the `pg_advisory_xact_lock` was deleted from the service** — it had never exercised serialization at all. Two rules follow. **Assert concurrency guarantees where they actually live — in the DATABASE**: a unique index can be tested here (insert the row a losing racer would write, expect the constraint to reject it), and unlike the advisory lock it also fails when you break it. **And prove any guard is load-bearing by REMOVING it and watching the test go red** — for a concurrency test that control is not optional, because passing-for-the-wrong-reason is the default outcome. Where a branch genuinely cannot be reached in PGlite (one transaction observing another's mid-flight insert), say so in the test file rather than writing a test that appears to cover it. **But saying so is where the note ENDS, not where the verification does — a lock-order question is answerable in about fifteen seconds outside the suite, so do not settle for "untestable here" when the claim is load-bearing.** `brew install postgresql@17`, then `initdb` into a `mktemp -d` and `pg_ctl -o "-p 55432 -k $TMP -c listen_addresses=''"` gives a throwaway real Postgres that touches nothing else on the machine; drive it with two `psql -f` processes backgrounded from one shell, interleaved with `SELECT pg_sleep(n)` so each side takes its locks in the order the code does. Measured 2026-09-02 on task `26316bcb`, which asked whether `createQuestion` and the multi-entry PowerSync upload could ABBA-deadlock against `deleteAssignee` on `ensureSelfAssignee`: the answer was **yes, with a real `deadlock detected` from Postgres**, and the same harness produced the negative controls that made it meaningful (`INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` does **not** block on a *committed* conflicting row — unlike `DO UPDATE` — but **does** block while another transaction holds that unique key in flight, which is the whole reason the window is narrow). Reading the code alone would have given neither the confirmation nor the boundary. Keep the driver script next to the test that cannot run it, so the finding stays re-verifiable instead of becoming folklore.

⚠️ **But do NOT read this bullet as «`Promise.all` proves nothing» — that over-reads it, and it cost a real regression a test.** What PGlite cannot give you is two TRANSACTIONS in flight at once, which is why the advisory-lock test above was vacuous. A **read-modify-write spread across two separate awaited calls** is a different animal and IS reproducible here, because PGlite serializes STATEMENTS, not call sequences: `Promise.all` over two route calls CAN interleave as read → read → write → write, which is exactly the window a validate-then-upsert leaves open. ⚠️ That ordering is not guaranteed by `Promise.all` — two handlers with different awaits before their read can still run read → write → read → write — so it is a race you can usually REACH, not one you can assume; verify it on the endpoint in question rather than reasoning it must hold. Measured 2026-09-04 on `money_deposit_terms`: two concurrent `PUT /api/money/deposits/:id/terms`, one naming `openedDate` and the other `maturityDate`, each valid against the same old row, deterministically returned **200/400** with the constraint-violation mapping in place and **200/500** with it removed. The author had written in review that the path was unreachable on this harness; `codex review` said otherwise and was right. **So before writing "not testable in PGlite", ask which KIND of race it is** — two transactions (genuinely out of reach; assert the guarantee in the schema and prove it against a throwaway real Postgres as above) or one value read and written across two calls (write the `Promise.all` test, and run the guard-removal control to prove it is load-bearing).

- **PowerSync sync rules** (`apps/powersync/config/sync-config.yaml`): data queries are **single-table — no JOINs** (PowerSync rejects them). There is exactly **ONE** bucket definition, `by_user`, parameterized by `request.jwt() ->> 'sub'`: every synced table carries a `user_id` and filters on `bucket.user_id`. `task_session_events`, `api_tokens`, and `device_auth_requests` are intentionally **outside** the sync set (events fetched on-demand via `GET /api/sessions/:id/events`; the auth tables hold secrets and never reach clients).

- **PowerSync buckets are capped at 1000 per connection, and a parent-id parameter query spends one bucket PER PARENT ROW.** Both `api.parameters.max_buckets_per_connection` and `max_parameter_query_results` default to 1000; crossing that count aborts **every** sync stream instantly (`[PSYNC_S2305]`, `data_sent_bytes: 0`) — a total client freeze on web _and_ mobile while writes keep persisting server-side and the health probes stay green. It reads as a feature bug, not a sync bug (2026-08-05: "a recurring task's next occurrence isn't spawned" — it was; the client never got the row). That outage came from a `by_task` bucket that enumerated the user's task ids; **fixed structurally 2026-08-08** — the seven task child tables now carry their own `user_id`, all live in `by_user`, and `by_task` is deleted, so bucket count no longer tracks task count. The 10000 ceilings in `service.yaml` remain as headroom, not as the mechanism. **So: prefer an owner column over a parent-id parameter query in any NEW bucket definition** — the trap is still live for anyone who adds one. Full symptoms + the six-step rollout an owner column needs on an already-synced table → the repo `railway` skill.
- **Every SYNCED table needs an `id` column — PowerSync rejects a data query that emits no `id`, so a
per-user singleton keyed on `user_id` alone cannot be synced.** The shape for a singleton is
`id uuid PK default gen_random_uuid()` + `user_id text NOT NULL UNIQUE` (`nanny_config`,
`money_config`, `rodovid_settings`); a `user_id` primary key is fine ONLY for server-only tables
such as `rodovid_sync_state`. Caught by `codex review` on the fifth round of the rodovid research
desk (2026-09-04), after four rounds and two reviewers had passed the `SELECT * FROM

lines.t: looked healthy, and only auth was dead. Check `dig clerk.plun.me` **and its CNAME target** against a
public resolver before reading a line of app code; a `ping` of the app's own domain proves nothing.
Three consequences make this cost hours if you skip it:
- **The Clerk SDK gives up PERMANENTLY.** It spends three retries within seconds of
`Application.onCreate` and then logs `Max initialization retries (3) reached. Initialization
failed permanently. Call Clerk.reinitialize() to retry manually.` A boot on a bad network
therefore leaves auth dead **for that process**, and fixing the network does not revive it — the
measured recovery was DNS restored → `am force-stop` → relaunch, i.e. a NEW process, which no
user is going to guess (an Activity restart does not do it; the process and its SDK state survive
one). `ClerkNativePlugin.reviveIfNeeded()` now makes the re-init call, on the sign-in TAP rather
than at boot — boot renders nothing while it waits, so reviving there would trade a wrong screen
for a blank one.
- **It presents as a LOGIN bug when nobody is logged out.** `Clerk.user` is a plain snapshot, so
reading it before the client loads returns null for a live session — the app then shows the
sign-in screen to a signed-in user, whose only button needs the very initialization that failed.
On that fresh process Yarik was back in **without the button ever being pressed**: the session had
been in storage the whole time. `isSignedIn` now reports `initialized` separately, because
«signed out» and «could not ask» are different answers owed different screens.
