lines.t: ## Load-bearing patterns

- **A zod/JS `.length` cap counts UTF-16 CODE UNITS, not characters — an emoji costs 2, so a text you measured in Python passes your check and fails the server's.** Measured 2026-09-10: a 1 997-code-POINT string was rejected as ">2000". It bites hardest where the truncation is silent — `recurrence.learnings` (20 000; appending past the cap drops the OLDEST entries) and task notes. Count with `len(s.encode('utf-16-le'))//2` before writing anything near a cap. ⚠️ **Not every cap here works that way, so do not "correct" one you have not read**: `decodeHeader` in `miniapps/rodovid/src/server.ts` clamps with `[...decoded].slice(0, limit)`, which is code POINTS, deliberately. The rule is about `.length`-based validators; anything spread-based is the other convention.

- **A finger produces no `hover:` — in the Capacitor WebView a `hover:`-only affordance is invisible, and a `.catch(() => {})` on the handler makes the failure look like a dead button.** Measured 2026-09-11 on «Увійти через Google»: the actual fault was a home-router NXDOMAIN on `frontend-api.clerk.services`, and one `adb logcat` line named it in a second — but the app swallowed the error, so from the screen it was indistinguishable from an unresponsive control. Two rules follow: read the DEVICE's own log before theorising about the UI, and **dump before you clear** — `adb logcat -c` wipes the device-wide buffer, including the single line written at process start that usually explains the whole thing.

- **User scoping**: every DB query is scoped by `userId` from the Clerk JWT or API token (`c.var.userId` in Hono). `tasks`, `task_sessions`, `assignees`, `api_tokens` carry an explicit `user_id` column; children are scoped via FK joins. Never read or write across users. The upload handler (`/api/powersync/upload`) inserts under the caller's user, whitelists which columns a client may set (never `id`/`user_id`/`task_id`), and scopes every update/delete to the caller — tasks by `user_id` (incl. a `setWhere` on the PUT conflict), child rows by the parent task's owner via an `exists` guard. Cross-table references are ownership-checked too: a task's `assignee_id` (REST or upload) must point at one of the caller's own `assignees` rows.

- **Batch upserts: collapse duplicate keys BEFORE the insert, and report the two kinds of duplicate separately.** Postgres `ON CONFLICT` cannot see a conflict *inside its own statement* — two rows carrying the same key in one `VALUES` list raise `21000` rather than being arbitrated — so any tool taking an array (`shopping_suggest` is the first) must de-duplicate on the way in. The subtler half, caught by its own test on 03.09.2026: an entry collapsed intra-batch shares its key with the sibling row that *was* created, so computing "what failed" as `input.filter(v => !createdKeys.has(v.key))` marks it **successful** and it vanishes silently. Track the intra-batch collapses separately and concatenate. `miniapps/shopping/src/mcp-silpo.ts`.

- **Reading a repo lock — "free" must be a POSITIVE answer, never the absence of one.** `GET /api/repo-locks` (or `list_git_locks`) is the only way to know whether another agent holds a working tree, and the obvious wait loop — grep the response for your path, treat "no match" as free — reports FREE on an empty body, a 502, or a dropped connection. Measured 2026-09-07: one blipped curl inside a poll declared the tree free while a night session was still writing in it, and the "wait" that produced it had been running correctly for the previous 45 minutes. Check the HTTP status is 200 and parse the JSON before believing either answer; on anything else the honest verdict is "I don't know", which is a different thing from "free". The same rule applies to the lock ITSELF: an agent that cannot take one (a day pane before `start_pair_session` existed, a human at the keyboard) is invisible to the protocol, so a clean `locks: []` means "nobody who asks is holding it", not "nobody is editing it".

- **To force a juggernaut-cli feature to FAIL against the API, point `JUGGERNAUT_PROFILES_FILE` at a scratch registry — `JUGGERNAUT_API_URL` alone silently does nothing.** The env var is honoured only for env- and file-sourced credentials (`connect-credentials.ts`); a profile discovered from a stored **MCP server entry** takes its `apiUrl` from that entry and ignores it, which is the normal shape on this machine. So the obvious negative control — re-run with `JUGGERNAUT_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9` and check the feature reports an outage — prints the ordinary healthy output and exit 0, indistinguishable from a guard that works. Measured 2026-09-10 building the `repo-locks` panel section: two negative controls in a row "passed" while never leaving prod. Write a scratch `{"agents":[{"id":"probe","label":"probe","token":"jg_probe","kind":"claude"}],"subscriptions":[]}` and `chmod 600` it — `loadProfileRegistry` **silently returns an empty registry for any file whose mode is not 0600**, and the feature then reports "no profiles" rather than the failure you were testing, which is a second way to think you ran a control when you did not. With that file in place, `JUGGERNAUT_API_URL` applies and both a socket failure and a 401 are reachable.

- **A local-first page that must write back a SERVER-computed value has no atomic path, so the write belongs on the server — do not try to close the windows from the client.** The shape: the browser reads a figure only the server can compute (it needs server-only rows), derives a new value from it, and writes the result through PowerSync. That is a read-modify-write across two stores with no transaction, and every gap is a way to persist a value that was never true — the fetch-to-tap gap, a row committed inside it, an un-uploaded local edit the server never saw, two taps interleaving, another tab writing mid-request. Measured 2026-09-09 on `/nanny`, where `balance_checkpoint` is a (balance, timestamp) PAIR the summary rolls forward from: the client paired a balance fetched ~35 s earlier with `Date.now()` at the tap, so each action silently discarded that gap's accrual — 10 ₴ over two expenses, reported as «хіба мало б бути не 4 гривні боргу?». **Eight rounds of cross-vendor review each closed one window and found the next**, which is the signature `development-process` names for a wrong model rather than a missing patch. The fix that ended it was `POST /api/nanny/balance-action`: the client sends only WHAT happened (`{kind, amount}`) and the server reads its own state, computes, and writes under `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` in one transaction, stamping the checkpoint with the same `now` the balance was computed for. Two riders the redesign still needs, and they are not optional: **drain `ps_crud` before the call** (the server is authoritative only over writes it has RECEIVED, and `dataFlowStatus.uploading` reads false before a queued transaction starts — `revalueAfterUpload` in `money-account-form.tsx` documents the same trap), and **carry an idempotency key**, because the local-first write being replaced was idempotent for free while an appending POST is not — replay a spent key with a CHANGED payload as a 409, never a 200, or an ambiguous retry closes the editor over an amount that was never recorded. Same shape is latent anywhere else a miniapp writes back a server-derived number.

- **One task, many child tables: the lock order is PARENT FIRST, always — and a joined `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` does NOT give you that.** `tasks` has `task_comments`, `task_suggestions`, `task_questions` and `task_suggestion_parks` hanging off it, and `deleteTask` plus every FK cascade goes parent-then-children, so nothing else may go the other way. Two traps, both of which look correct on the page. **(a) A joined `FOR UPDATE` over a child and its parent locks them in whatever order the PLAN yields** — a PK-driven nested loop takes the CHILD first — so `resolveSuggestionInTx` and `answerQuestion` were both inverted against task deletion while reading as if they locked the task. The shape that works is: resolve the parent id on an UNLOCKED read (which takes no row lock and so cannot invert anything), `lockOwnedTask`, then re-read the child under `FOR UPDATE OF <child>` and decide nothing on the unlocked read. **(b) Inserting a child takes a key-share lock on the parent through the FK**, so any later `FOR UPDATE` on that same parent row is a lock UPGRADE and deadlocks against a holder — which is what the comment routes did once posting a comment started reaching for the task. `lockOwnedTask` (`services/suggestion-parking.ts`) is the primitive and carries the rule; re-taking a lock you already hold is free. **None of this is testable in the suite** (PGlite serialises everything over one connection — see the `Promise.all` bullet above), and all four inversions were found by cross-vendor review rather than by tests, so treat a review finding here as the primary evidence. The check lives in `apps/api/test/manual/suggestion-parking-lock-order.sh`, the sibling of `abba-repro.sh`: nine cases on a throwaway real PostgreSQL, each fix paired with the old shape it replaces so every one is shown to genuinely deadlock. ⚠️ **A shell harness that classifies on the ABSENCE of `deadlock detected` calls a dead server "clean"** — the first version of that script reported PASS on cases 2 and 3 while PostgreSQL had failed to start. A clean verdict must additionally require both sessions to exit 0 and print their commit markers.

- **Agent permission model**: API-token actors (`c.var.actor != null`) may only set task status `todo/in_progress/paused/blocked/plan_review` and reassign — `done`/`cancelled`, priority, title and `completedAt` are **human-only** (`assertAgentTaskUpdateAllowed` in `services/tasks.ts`; the PowerSync upload rejects agent tokens outright). `model`/`effort` are human-only on UPDATE too, but an agent MAY set them at CREATION (`createTaskBody`, MCP `create_task`; coerced against the assignee's kind like PATCH) — Yarik, 2026-09-08. Agents propose those via `task_suggestions` (REST `POST /api/tasks/:id/suggestions`, MCP `suggest_change`); resolution (`POST /api/suggestions/:id/resolve`) is human-only and applies the change with actor null in one tx. **An unresolved suggestion PARKS its task in `awaiting_input`**, the same place an unanswered question parks it — the pre-park status is kept in the server-only `task_suggestion_parks` (migration 0159, never synced) and restored on a reject, with `in_progress` restored as `todo` so a resurrected claim cannot slip past the one-in-progress guard. An agent status write on a parked task is dropped for everything but `in_progress`. **Any HUMAN action withdraws every pending suggestion as `superseded`** — a published comment (REST or the PowerSync upload; a draft does not count, publishing it does, and the web's duplicate write of one comment fires once) or a real edit to title/status/priority/assignee/notes/**model/effort** (the last two are why the predicate is `humanEditedTaskProperties` and not `recordTaskChanges`, which does not audit them). Answering a question and accepting a suggestion are both human actions and withdraw the rest; a plain reject is not. `superseded` is a distinct status precisely so the timeline does not render an automatic withdrawal as «@me declined … proposal». A loop's `done` is auto-accepted only while NOTHING else on the task is pending, so an iteration never closes over an unanswered question. All of it lives in `services/suggestion-parking.ts`. `completedAt` is stamped server-side on the done transition (REST + upload paths) — clients never send it. **Plan-review loop**: an agent submits a plan by posting it (session summary/comment) and setting `plan_review` + `@me`; the task page's review panel approves or rejects-with-feedback via local-first writes that return the task to `todo` + the plan author (`nextTask` only serves `todo`, so `plan_review` parks tasks out of agent queues).

- **Assignee registry**: tasks reference `assignees` (per-user roster) via `tasks.assignee_id` — no assignee enum on tasks. Every user has an undeletable `@me` row (kind `human`), **lazily upserted** by `ensureSelfAssignee` (assignees list, task create, upload default). Deleting an assignee reassigns their tasks to `@me` **and revokes its bound token**. Cosmetic identity (`display_name`, `avatar` — a ≤96KB data-URL set via `PUT /api/assignees/:id/avatar`) is agent-self-editable (own row only); the canonical `name` is human-only. Assignee writes are **API-only**; PowerSync syncs the table down read-only. Agent roster names can never collide with human rows (`ensureAgentAssignee` refuses, incl. `@me`).

- **Malformed uuid path params are screened per-resolver, at exactly the point the route already resolves a valid-but-unknown id.** `isUuid` (`apps/api/src/uuid.ts`) guards a resolver so a malformed id 404s instead of reaching Postgres and 500ing on `invalid input syntax for type uuid`. **Coverage is per-resolver and NOT complete** — the tasks/sessions/questions/suggestions/assignees/oauth/token resolvers are screened, but `apps/api/test/malformed-uuid-params.test.ts` only exercises the **task-id, session-id and assignee-id** families — a regression in the question-answer, suggestion-resolve, OAuth-client or token-revoke guards would keep the suite green. The subscription usage routes (`POST /:id/usage`, `GET /:id/usage/history`, `/usage/series`) still pass the raw param into `eq(subscriptions.id, …)` and therefore still 500. Screen them when you next touch them; don't assume a route is covered because this rule exists. **The invariant is equivalence, not a fixed position in the handler**: a malformed id and a **valid-but-unknown** uuid must return the SAME status (`apps/api/test/malformed-uuid-params.test.ts`) — which is also what stops a "fixed" 404 from being a coincidence. So place the check immediately before the first SQL use of that id and let it inherit whatever precedence the route already has: on body-bearing routes that call `ensureTaskOwned` first (comments, sessions) an unknown task 404s before the body is ever parsed, so the screen belongs there too, ahead of the payload check. The failure mode is moving it EARLIER than that point: hoisted above an ownership/permission check it turns 403 into 404; hoisted above a body parse on a route that validates the body first it turns 400 into 404. Screening where the resolver actually consumes the id is what keeps both contracts intact.

- **`useQuery`'s `isLoading` is the INITIAL load only — when the PARAMETERS change it re-evaluates with `isLoading` already false, `isFetching` true, and `data` still holding the PREVIOUS parameters' rows. So `!isLoading && rows.length > 0` does not mean "these are the rows for what I just asked".** The natural use is a "the id I was given isn't there, so drop the URL parameter" redirect, and that is exactly where it destroys a deep link: navigating from person A to `/medical?profile=B&form=<a pill of B's>` looks B's pill up in A's retained rows, misses, and erases a perfectly valid `form` parameter before B's rows arrive. The types say it plainly (`ReadonlyQueryResult`, @powersync/react 1.10) — *"Loading becomes false once the first set of results … is available"* vs *"is true … any time when the query is re-evaluating"* — and `reportFetching` defaults to **true** (`WatchedQuery.js`), so the flag is really populated and costs nothing to read. **Gate any "the row genuinely does not exist" conclusion on `!isLoading && !isFetching`.** A plain render is fine on stale rows (that is what makes them a feature); it is the IRREVERSIBLE act — a redirect, a delete, a "create it then" — that must wait. Caught by `codex review` on the /medical person-page reorder (11.09.2026); the pre-existing code it was moved from had the same gap.

- **PowerSync web hands out ONE exclusive connection lease per origin AND database file, shared by every tab that opens that database, with a 120 s default lock timeout — so any local read is at the mercy of a tab you are not looking at, and a poller without an in-flight guard makes it worse.** Which primitive enforces it depends on the configuration — desktop multi-tab serialises inside a shared worker, the dedicated-worker fallback takes a navigator lock — so do NOT reason from one of them; the durable fact is the SCOPE: contention needs the origin and the database file to match. Given the per-Clerk-user `juggernaut-<userId>.db` rule below, that means the tabs fighting each other are always the same user's, on the same host. `getUploadQueueStats()` (and anything else taking that lease) waits behind whoever holds it, and the wait is four times longer than the 30 s queue-poll cadence. A `setInterval` that fires regardless therefore stacks waiters behind its own outstanding read, and their failures then arrive together and get counted as independent evidence — measured over 19–24.08 on the desktop watcher: 82 of 958 neighbouring `could not read upload queue stats` rows under two seconds apart, two of them **2 ms** apart from one tab, which one 30 s poller cannot produce. Chrome's background-tab timer throttling is the other half: the median gap between neighbouring failed polls was 60.5 s against a requested 30 s, so **anything computed as `ticks × interval` is fiction — derive durations from clock readings.** The fix pattern is in `apps/web/src/powersync/uploadQueueWatch.ts`: skip the tick while a read is in flight, and declare a detector blind on ELAPSED TIME rather than on a completion count, or the guard silently makes the detector slower and a read that never returns produces no log line at all.

- **Reading an upload-queue blind report: `skippedTicks` is the tab's LIVENESS PROOF, no field names the lease HOLDER, and a quiet window after a tab RELOAD is not evidence that anything was fixed.** `beginTick` (`apps/web/src/powersync/uploadQueueWatch.ts`) increments `skippedTicks` only when the poll timer actually fires with a read still outstanding, so `skippedTicks: 3` on a `queue_watch_blind` means the tab ran three times *during its own blind window* — a frozen tab or a slept Mac cannot produce it, which makes it the positive liveness signal `visible` cannot give (per the bullet above, macOS sleep never fires `visibilitychange`). Measured 2026-08-28 07:37Z, the only blind episode in the 74 h after `ded2be2`: two desktop tabs on `juggernaut.plun.me`, both `reason: no_answer`, `consecutive: 0`, `err: null`, `skippedTicks: 3`, `inFlightForMs` 90 003 and 119 989 — both awake and ticking while their reads went unanswered, the second right up to the SDK's 120 s lock timeout, i.e. the same wait that used to surface as `TimeoutError: signal timed out`. **So a blind report describes the WAITER and only the waiter.** Its `url` says nothing about who holds the lease — at that moment the same origin+database also carried a backgrounded `/money/income` tab armed six hours earlier — so "the blind tab was on /agents" does NOT clear the money routes; naming the holder needs instrumentation on the HOLDING side, which the waiter-side fields structurally cannot supply. And before crediting any fix here, check for a reload: the symptom's 2026-08-25 20:11:58Z stop was one (last warn 20:11:58, `queue_watch_sighted` 20:12:21, fresh `queue_watch_armed` 20:12:55) — a full day BEFORE the fix deployed, because the symptom lives in a tab's AGE and reloading resets it. Normalise any before/after count by desktop `queue_watch_armed` per day, or a quiet week merely means the browser was not left open.

- **Reading the PowerSync reconnect watchdog's logs: `downForMs` is ACCUMULATED downtime, never stall duration — always pair a `reconnect_forced` with the `reconnect_recovered` that follows it before calling anything stuck.** The watchdog (`apps/web/src/powersync/reconnectWatchdog.ts`, component `powersync.watchdog`) stamps `downForMs` with wall-clock time since the connection last went down, which on a backgrounded phone or a slept laptop is mostly time the process wasn't running. Measured 2026-08-21: a `reconnect_forced` carrying `downForMs: 5421890` (**90 min**) and another at **73.7 min** were each followed by `reconnect_recovered` **2 seconds later** — i.e. the watchdog worked perfectly and a `downForMs`-only reading would have reported a 90-minute outage that never happened. Two companion traps in the same rows: `visible: true` does **not** mean a human was looking (macOS sleep never fires `visibilitychange`, so a slept Mac logs `visible: true` throughout), and `reconnect_attempt_error: "Operation aborted by abort controller"` is the watchdog's own 30 s timeout firing, not a network fault. And because `clientLogger` hardcodes `service: 'juggernaut-web'` for the mobile WebView too, **split desktop from mobile by `userAgent`, never by `service`** — in that same window 26 of 27 "visible-tab stalls" were the Android app, not the web app the ticket was about. **Two more splits the same sweep needs.** Frontend custom fields are NESTED: `clientLogger` puts everything a call site passes under a single `context` object (`apps/web/src/lib/clientLogger.ts`), so only `dt`/`level`/`message`/`component`/`userId`/`url`/`userAgent`/`source`/`service` are top-level — a query reading `JSONExtractString(raw,'watchId')` returns an **empty string, not an error**, which reads exactly like a field that was never shipped. Use `JSONExtractString(raw,'context','<field>')`. And the app is served from **two origins** (`plun.me` and `juggernaut.plun.me`, the former carrying most desktop traffic since 21.08), which are two separate local databases — so a desktop sweep must split on the `url` host as well as on `userAgent`.

- **Test auth**: `apps/api/src/app.ts` accepts the auth middleware as a parameter so tests can swap in a stub that reads `x-test-user` instead of verifying a real Clerk JWT. The route handlers themselves never know the difference. **A cross-user isolation test must use ONE harness and the `x-test-user` header — a second `buildHarness()` is a second PGlite instance, i.e. a different database, so "the other user" writes somewhere the assertion can never see.** Such a test does not fail loudly; it passes for the wrong reason. Measured 2026-08-28 on the shopping appliers: two isolation tests failed (the foreign row simply wasn't there to be protected), and a third — "rejects an item filed under another user's group" — went GREEN because the foreign group id matched no row at all, so it proved only that an unknown id is rejected, never that ownership is checked. The tell is an isolation assertion whose setup ran through a harness other than the one under test. Pair every such test with a **positive control** in the same body (the same write against the caller's OWN row must succeed, and the owner's own delete must work), or a 400 that means "always rejected" is indistinguishable from one that means "not yours".

- **`tx.execute(sql\`…\`)` returns a DRIVER-DEPENDENT shape — postgres-js hands back an array of rows, PGlite hands back `{ rows: [...] }` — so `result[0]` works in prod and silently finds nothing in the test suite.** Reach for a raw `execute` and the natural place is a `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, which the query builder hides behind `.for('update')`; the builder version is typed, portable, and has no shape to get wrong, so prefer it and keep `execute` for statements with no rows to read. The failure is nastier than a crash because it is silently ASYMMETRIC: measured 2026-09-12 on `POST /api/attack/override`, every happy-path test 404'd (the locked row read as absent) while every validation test passed, since those return before the transaction — which reads like a missing fixture or a broken seed, not like a driver difference. Note what this means for the general rule two bullets down: a harness that is "the same database" in every way you normally check can still disagree with prod about the shape of a result, so a test failing ONLY on the paths that reach the database deserves a look at the driver before a look at the data.

- **PGlite runs every query over ONE serialized connection, so `Promise.all` in a test is INTERLEAVED, not concurrent — a "race" test written that way passes whether or not the locking exists.** The harness (`apps/api/test/harness.ts`) is a single in-process instance; there is no second connection for a second transaction to run in. Measured 2026-08-29 while adding `agent_repo_locks`: a test firing three simultaneous acquires and asserting exactly one wins stayed **green after the `pg_advisory_xact_lock` was deleted from the service** — it had never exercised serialization at all. Two rules follow. **Assert concurrency guarantees where they actually live — in the DATABASE**: a unique index can be tested here (insert the row a losing racer would write, expect the constraint to reject it), and unlike the advisory lock it also fails when you break it. **And prove any guard is load-bearing by REMOVING it and watching the test go red** — for a concurrency test that control is not optional, because passing-for-the-wrong-reason is the default outcome. Where a branch genuinely cannot be reached in PGlite (one transaction observing another's mid-flight insert), say so in the test file rather than writing a test that appears to cover it. **But saying so is where the note ENDS, not where the verification does — a lock-order question is answerable in about fifteen seconds outside the suite, so do not settle for "untestable here" when the claim is load-bearing.** `brew install postgresql@17`, then `initdb` into a `mktemp -d` and `pg_ctl -o "-p 55432 -k $TMP -c listen_addresses=''"` gives a throwaway real Postgres that touches nothing else on the machine; drive it with two `psql -f` processes backgrounded from one shell, interleaved with `SELECT pg_sleep(n)` so each side takes its locks in the order the code does. Measured 2026-09-02 on task `26316bcb`, which asked whether `createQuestion` and the multi-entry PowerSync upload could ABBA-deadlock against `deleteAssignee` on `ensureSelfAssignee`: the answer was **yes, with a real `deadlock detected` from Postgres**, and the same harness produced the negative controls that made it meaningful (`INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` does **not** block on a *committed* conflicting row — unlike `DO UPDATE` — but **does** block while another transaction holds that unique key in flight, which is the whole reason the window is narrow). Reading the code alone would have given neither the confirmation nor the boundary. Keep the driver script next to the test that cannot run it, so the finding stays re-verifiable instead of becoming folklore.

steps.label: A KEYSET CURSOR must compare INSIDE Postgres — round-tripping the boundary timestamp through JS breaks it twice, and the second break survives the fix for the first.

lines.t: - **Prefer the Drizzle query builder over `db.execute` — the raw-SQL escape hatch returns a DIFFERENT SHAPE in tests than in prod, and both typecheck.** `Database` is typed as `PostgresJsDatabase`, but the test harness passes a `PgliteDatabase`, and their `execute` results disagree: measured 2026-08-24, PGlite returns `{ rows, fields, affectedRows }` and is **not iterable**, while postgres-js returns the row list itself. So `for (const r of await db.execute(...))` or `[...result]` throws `is not iterable` in the suite while being correct in production — or, worse, the reverse for code shaped the other way, which ships a green suite over a broken read. There is currently **no `db.execute` anywhere in `miniapps/` or `apps/api/src`**, and that is worth keeping: `db.select({ ... })` with `sql` expressions for the computed columns (plus `groupBy`) covers the aggregate cases and normalises the result across both drivers. If you genuinely need raw SQL, read `.rows` defensively and test it on BOTH drivers rather than trusting the type.

- **Never interpolate a JS `Date` (or any non-primitive) into a raw `` sql`` `` template — encode it first. This is the same PGlite-vs-postgres-js split as the bullet above, one level down, and it is worse because the suite is structurally incapable of catching it.** Drizzle encodes a value only when it knows the COLUMN; inside a `` sql`` `` template it binds with the **noop encoder**, so the value reaches the driver exactly as written. postgres.js then throws `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE … Received an instance of Date`, while **PGlite accepts the raw Date and the test passes**. Measured 2026-08-24: the music library-pass job failed on **every tick from the moment the miniapp shipped** (100 %, zero pages persisted) because its re-like guard interpolated `${track.addedAt}` — and the column-typed `addedAt` two lines above, same value, was encoded to an ISO string and worked. Two `library pass` tests exercise that exact statement and stayed green the whole time. So: write `${d.toISOString()}` (the repo's other two Date-derived interpolations already do), and where a raw template is unavoidable on a hot path, **test it by compiling the statement on the PRODUCTION dialect and asserting on `toSQL().params`** — `apps/api/test/music-collector-params.test.ts` is the worked pattern: it needs no database, is blind to the driver split, and goes red on the unencoded version. The general rule this is the second instance of: **a green suite proves nothing about a code path whose behaviour differs between the test driver and the prod driver — the assertion has to move to something both share**, which here is the compiled query.

- **A KEYSET CURSOR must compare INSIDE Postgres — round-tripping the boundary timestamp through JS breaks it twice, and the second break survives the fix for the first.** Measured 2026-09-16 adding paging to `rodovid_questions_list` (task 76c5cef2), where both were caught in review rather than by tests. (a) The natural spelling `sql\`(${col.createdAt}, ${col.id}) > (${createdAt}, ${id})\`` is the Date-interpolation bug in the bullet above, so it 500s in prod and passes on PGlite. (b) Encoding that Date correctly is still wrong: `timestamptz` holds MICROSECONDS and a JS `Date` holds milliseconds, so a cursor read into one and sent back rounds DOWN, the boundary row compares as still-greater and comes back again — with `limit: 1` the cursor never advances and the sweep loops for ever. The shape that works reads the timestamp back as a scalar subquery, so the only bound parameters are the cursor id and the user id, both strings: `questionCursorPredicate` in `miniapps/rodovid/src/research.ts`, guarded by `apps/api/test/rodovid-question-cursor-params.test.ts` (compiles on the postgres-js dialect, asserts no bound param is a `Date`) plus a pagination test that seeds three rows sharing a millisecond and **asserts via `to_char(created_at,'US')` that PGlite really stored them apart** — without that control the id tie-break alone pages them correctly and the test passes without exercising the case it exists for. ⚠️ **And inside a raw `sql` template an ALIASED table renders as the ALIAS NAME ALONE** — `from ${alias}` emits `from "my_alias"`, a relation that does not exist, while the alias's COLUMNS are qualified correctly; spell the FROM out as `from ${table} ${sql.identifier('my_alias')}`. All three failures look identical from the test suite, which is why the assertion has to be on the compiled SQL.

- **A SAMPLE of vendor telemetry that never shows a field is evidence about the SAMPLE — never write "this vendor always reports X as 0" from a convenient slice.** Sibling of the fixture-size rule below, one axis over: there the slice is too small to exercise a policy, here it is too small to contain a VALUE, and the resulting claim reads as a measured fact rather than a guess. Measured 2026-09-12 while pricing codex rounds: a 40-rollout slice reported `cache_write_input_tokens` as 0 in **all 909** of its usage records, which was about to be written into the pricing formula's comments as settled; the full corpus (`~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl`, 7 403 files, 233 516 records) has **13 520 non-zero** ones, up to 18.6M tokens each. The formula shipped on the small sample charged every cache-write token at 2.25x, and only `juggernaut review` questioned it. Two rules: **scan the whole corpus when it is local and the grep is cheap** (it was seconds here), and **state the denominator beside any "always/never" claim about vendor data**, so the next reader can see what it rests on. The positive form is what settled the same question: `cached + cacheWrite <= input` held in 4 531 of 4 531 records, which is what makes "both cache buckets are inside `input_tokens`" a finding rather than a reading of the docs.

- **A fixture SMALL enough to be readable can make a scale-dependent policy look correct — when the code embodies a POLICY whose payoff is emergent, measure the outcome over a simulated run, then re-measure with the mechanism removed.** Sibling of the two driver-split rules above, one axis over: there the suite and prod disagree about the DRIVER, here about the SIZE. Measured 2026-08-27 on the music duel's pair picker. Its job is to make a top-30 reachable out of 5 356 tracks in a few hundred answers; it always opened a question with a never-dealt track, matched against the placed track nearest its strength. Every unit test passed, and so did a 40-item simulation — because in a 40-item pool the supply of fresh tracks RUNS OUT, after which placed tracks start meeting each other. At real scale it never runs out: side A is permanently at strength 0, its opponent is permanently "whoever is nearest 0", and a track that wins twice moves away from 0 and is **never asked about again** — dying one duel short of the three a placement needs. Caught only by `codex review` reasoning about the real pool size, then confirmed by re-running the 300-item simulation, where the true best track finished **second** behind a middling anchor. The fix (alternate a coverage round with a promotion round) is pinned by a test that asserts an OUTCOME — a full top-30 after 100 answers, and the true top-5 in order — and goes red when the promotion round is disabled. **So: for a heuristic, "the tests pass" is not evidence; the assertion has to be a measured outcome at a realistic size, with a control run that has the mechanism switched off.**

- **A hand-written fake of an external service encodes an ERROR CONTRACT you guessed — and where the guess is wrong, the fixture and the code agree with each other and both disagree with prod.** Third axis of the two rules above: there the suite and prod disagree about the DRIVER or the SIZE, here about **what the upstream does when there is nothing to return**. The happy path is copied from a real response and is usually right; the miss is invented, and nothing ever checks it. Measured 2026-09-08 on rodovid: the fake for `GET /people/?gramps_id=…` answered a non-match with `200 []`, so `findPersonByGrampsId` looked correct, while the deployed gramps-web-api 3.18.0 answers a filtered collection matching nothing with **404** — which propagated as `Gramps returned 404 for GET /api/people/`, read as an unsupported endpoint, and cost an investigation ticket. The callers' own «No person with Gramps id X» could never fire, because the lookup threw first. **So when you fake a service, get its NEGATIVE cases from the wire, not from intuition** — one authenticated `curl` per case, recorded with its date in the deploy README next to the other measured limitations (`deploy/rodovid/README.md`). And distinguishing "supported filter, no match" from "unsupported filter" is itself a positive/negative control pair: an unknown filter there is `422 Unknown field`, a known one with no match is `404`, a known one with a match is `200`. ⚠️ **Scope any status you then decide to swallow to the REQUEST, never to the number alone** — a login happens inside the same call, so a misconfigured base URL 404s `POST /token/` too, and catching that as "not found" reports a missing row for a broken deployment. `GrampsError.request` carries a structured `{method, path}` for exactly this, per the "structured metadata, never message parsing" rule below.

- **A rule that reads an OPTIONAL column is verified only for the state that column is in today — and a column being backfilled will silently invert it.** Sibling of the driver-split and fixture-size rules around it, one axis over again: there the suite and prod disagree about the DRIVER or the SIZE, here about **how much data has arrived yet**. Measured 2026-09-07 on the music duel's `song-identity.ts`. It read Spotify's ISRC as the recording's identity in BOTH directions — same ISRC one song, several ISRCs several songs — with a title+artist+duration fallback "while ISRC is still unbackfilled". Both halves shipped green on 2026-08-30 and the duplicates really did disappear, because at that moment `isrc` was NULL everywhere and only the fallback ever ran. The collector then filled the column in, one reconcile at a time, and each merged group split apart again: a label re-registers an ISRC **per RELEASE**, so one master on a single and on the album carries several, and the premise "different ISRC ⇒ different recording" is simply false of Spotify's catalogue. Eight days later prod was back to **40 duplicate groups over 82 rows** — the same population the original fix removed — with no error, no failing test and no deploy in between. The tell that generalises: **a fallback path described as temporary is the path your tests are actually exercising**, so write the case where the optional value IS present and DISAGREES, and ask what the rule does the day the column is full. And prefer an asymmetric reading of any third-party identifier — here the fix was that ISRC only ever JOINS two rows, never SPLITS them, because "the vendor says these are the same" is trustworthy in a way "the vendor gave them different ids" is not.

- **Never build an error message from `String(err)` on a spawned child — Node puts the FULL argv in it, so anything secret in the argv is now in your logs.** `execFile`'s rejection message is `Command failed: <cmd> <argv joined>` (verified 2026-08-26), and `apps/cli` spawns herdr with `--env JUGGERNAUT_CLAUDE_TOKEN=jg_…` — so the obvious `catch (err) { message: String(err) }` writes a live roster key onto the `juggernaut start` panel and into `juggernaut start > log.txt`. It reads as harmless boilerplate, which is why it survived review twice. The fix belongs at the ONE place the message is built, not at each call site that renders it: `herdr()` in `apps/cli/src/herdr.ts` now returns `herdrCommandLabel(args)` (subcommand only, stops at the first flag) and `herdr.test.ts` drives a real failing call to assert the token is absent. Same rule for any future child process carrying a credential in its arguments — and prefer passing the secret via `env` where the API allows, since an argv is also visible in `ps`.

- **Code shared between `apps/web` and the server lives in `@juggernaut/platform` behind a SUBPATH export, never the package index.** The index pulls in hono, drizzle and pino, which have no business in a browser bundle — so `packages/platform/src/duel-fit.ts` is exported as `@juggernaut/platform/duel-fit` and imported by that path from both sides. The rule exists because the alternative is worse than it looks: the duel RATING is the same Bradley–Terry fit for /books, /movies, the /music page and the top-100 playlist job, and the second implementation that "temporarily" appeared on the server came with a test asserting the two agreed — a duplication with a guard bolted on, which `tsc` correctly refused (a backend test cannot import from `apps/web`: `rootDir`). If a shared thing needs a server-only dependency it does not belong in a subpath module at all.
- **Backend logs**: pino JSON to stdout, never `console.log`. Every state-changing route emits a log line at the end with `event: '<domain>.<action>'` plus relevant IDs.

- **A thrown `HTTPException` NEVER reaches an outer middleware's `catch` — Hono converts it to a response at the dispatch level of the handler that threw, so every handled 4xx used to be invisible by construction.** `compose()` (hono/dist/compose.js) wraps EACH middleware level in its own try/catch and calls `onError` there, sets `context.res`, and returns normally — so `logMiddleware`'s `await next()` never throws and the request records only `request.end status:400`, with no reason anywhere. `app.onError` returned the response without logging, so this was true of the WHOLE API, not one route. It cost 11 days on four paired 400s (task `5d7f6a24`) whose diagnosis was blocked on exactly this. `app.onError` now emits one `request.rejected` line (`apps/api/src/app.ts`); **`onError` is the only place a handled error object still exists, so any future per-status diagnostics belong there, not in the log middleware.** Pinned by `apps/api/test/request-rejected-logging.test.ts`, which goes red if the call is removed.

- **When one FIELD carries two meanings, tests that assert its value cannot tell them apart — and a green suite over such a fixture is what lets an ambiguity survive its own fix.** Sibling of the rules above, but the blind spot is in the EXPECTATION rather than the driver or the scale: the assertion is literally correct for both readings, so nothing is left to go red. Measured 2026-09-01 on the nanny cash banner (task 7aae958e). `computeCashRunsOutDate` returned `today` both for "today is the last day cash covers" and for "cash does not cover today", the page inferred the second from `date === today`, and it announced «Готівки вже недостатньо» on a day with 765 ₴ of planned spend against 1565 ₴ free. Three tests asserted `'2026-07-01'` — today in that fixture — across BOTH meanings, and they had been written days earlier by the session that fixed the previous bug in the same function, under a `codex review` and a full green suite. The tell is a value that is simultaneously a boundary (today, zero, the first or last element) and the answer: `date === today` cannot be both the datum and the discriminator. **The fix is to split the field, not to sharpen the test** — a client that must infer which case a value means will eventually infer wrong. Then pin the pair: two cases sharing the DATE and differing only in the new flag, and re-run them with the split reverted to prove they go red.

- **Never log an error MESSAGE you did not construct — log structured metadata instead. No analysis of a finished string can separate its static half from an interpolated one.** 47 `HTTPException` throw sites in `apps/api/src` interpolate something, and a few interpolate user content (a submitted free-text question answer in `services/questions.ts`, an attachment filename in `services/attachments.ts`). Two redaction attempts were written and each was defeated in `codex review` within one round — quote-delimited spans (a filename may contain `"`), then a lowercase-snake_case allowlist (`my secret password` and an extensionless `passport` both pass it). What IS safe is structure: a zod error reduces to `path:code` pairs (`zodIssueSummary` in `middleware/log.ts`), which names the failing FIELD and provably cannot carry its value. If a specific throw site ever needs its reason in the logs, give it structured metadata on the exception's `cause` — do not re-derive it from the text.
- **Frontend logs**: import `clientLogger` from `src/lib/clientLogger.ts` — singleton, batches to BetterStack in prod, console-only in dev. Wired to `window.onerror` and `unhandledrejection`.
- **No mocks of internal code**: backend tests run against a real Postgres (PGlite in tests, real Postgres in dev/prod). Only the auth boundary is swapped.
- **No `.js` extensions in workspace package imports**: drizzle-kit's loader can't follow them. Use extensionless imports inside `packages/db-schema/`.

- **Deployed ≠ callable in this process (MCP tool list is process-cached)**: a newly-deployed juggernaut MCP tool can't be called from the long-running Claude Code process that shipped it — the MCP client caches `tools/list` at connect time and doesn't refresh per cron tick (ToolSearch won't find it; existing tools keep their old schemas too). **Reassigning the task to another agent kind does NOT reliably make the tool callable sooner** — observed twice (Jun 2026): after shipping `ask_user`, three consecutive Codex/Cowork runs (incl. a _fresh_ Cowork session 24h later) still couldn't see it — only a full **MCP client reconnect** surfaced it; and the new `vinyl_*` tools stayed invisible to Cowork on reassignment, appearing only ~40 min later while other tools were present. So a new tool can stay invisible to **every** live session — including fresh ones and other agent kinds — for tens of minutes until that client's MCP connection actually reconnects. Practical rule: **don't promise a same-tick dogfood and don't assume "reassign to Cowork" picks it up**; drive the new endpoint via the **REST API** (the reliable fallback) until a session actually surfaces the tool, and only then dogfood the MCP path. Same family as the plugin-version-bump gotcha above ("deployed ≠ visible in this process"), and as the running-vs-installed trap for long-lived local binaries (→ `development-process` step 7).

- **An identity may not be decided by EVIDENCE THAT MOVES — a tie-break on duel counts is not a tie-break, it is a slow rename.** Sibling of the optional-column rule above, one axis over: there the input arrives later, here it never stops changing. Measured 2026-09-09 while unioning the album pool with the Discogs shelf. A shelf row can match two `music_album` records — «V.A.N» credited to `Bad Omens / Poppy` against a `Bad Omens` row and a `Poppy` row, which are two groups because their artist sets differ — and the first fix arbitrated with the same «most duels, ties to the smallest id» rule `groupAlbums`/`groupSongs` use to pick a CANONICAL row. That rule is sound there and wrong here: picking which of several rows STANDS for one record is stable under a growing log, while deciding WHICH RECORD a row is is not. Two claimants starting level go to the smallest id; one more unrelated verdict about the other flips it, and the record — with every verdict written against it — migrates to a different album while neither catalogue changed. **The fix was to stop resolving and start representing**: the MARK («чи є він у мене на полиці») is answered for every claimant, the IDENTITY is refused, and a verdict against an ambiguous row stays as written for `fitStrengths` to ignore, exactly as before the union. The guarantee is structural rather than a convention — `bindShelfToGroups` takes only the shelf and the groups, so the duel log is not in scope and no later edit there can reintroduce the dependency. **The general test before writing a tie-break: would this answer be the same next week if the user changed nothing but kept using the app?**

- **The behavioral marker for "the API's new revision is live" (step 7) is `deployCommit`, read via the MCP `mcp_status` tool** (also present in the `mcpServer` block of every `get_task` response) — **there is no REST equivalent**: `/api/mcp/status` does not exist. A polling loop that hits that path 40 times gets an empty string back every time, which reads exactly like "deploy stuck" while the deploy is actually already live — precisely the instrument-vs-target trap `development-process` step 7 warns about (an empty result is a claim about the INSTRUMENT, not about the deploy). Use `mcp_status`/`get_task`'s `deployCommit` to confirm an **API** push has landed, not a REST poll. ⚠️ **And if you poll it over raw JSON-RPC, note the payload is an ESCAPED JSON STRING** — `tools/call` returns `{"result":{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"{\n  \"deployCommit\": \"…\"}"}]}}`, so the natural `grep -o '"deployCommit":"[a-f0-9]*"'` matches nothing: there is a space after the colon and every quote is backslashed. Measured 2026-09-09 — a 24-iteration poll printed an empty string every time while the deploy had in fact landed at iteration two, i.e. the loop reported «stuck» for eight minutes about its own regex. Parse the `text` field (`json.loads` it) rather than grepping the envelope — **and note the field is NESTED under `mcpServer`, not at the top level of that decoded object**: `json.loads(text)['mcpServer']['deployCommit']`. Reading it off the root returns empty, which is indistinguishable from the escaping bug above and from a stalled deploy, so the same loop fails the same way a second time. Measured again 2026-09-09, one commit later: a 40-iteration poll that DID decode the text correctly still printed an empty string for ten minutes while the deploy had landed — this time about its own key path. And a THIRD spelling of the same mistake, 2026-09-11: a poll that decoded the text AND used the right key path still never terminated, because it compared the answer against the **short** sha from `git log --oneline` while `deployCommit` returns the **full 40-character** one — the loop ran past its ten-minute timeout while the deploy had been live for minutes. Three instruments, three different wrong answers, all reading «stuck». **The generalisation is that every failure here has been in the READER, never in the deploy — so make the loop print what it actually got on each iteration, and compare with a prefix match (`deployCommit.startswith(sha)`) rather than equality.** A poll that prints nothing cannot tell you whether it is looking at an empty string, a full sha or the previous revision. **Scope it to the API**: a web-only change need not rebuild the API, so `deployCommit` can keep reading the old commit after the web revision is already live — for a web-only deploy, verify with the bundle-hash flip instead (already the rule in `juggernaut-ops:codebase-simplify-pass` step 4).

- **PowerSync local tables can go transiently EMPTY** on the client (a sync reconciliation clears local rows; on mobile the whole local database can disappear between boots). Two corrections measured 2026-08-01/02, both of which had misdirected earlier debugging: the web SDK stores each `dbFilename` as an **IndexedDB** database (the default `IDBBatchAtomicVFS`), **not OPFS** — an OPFS-only inventory looks reassuringly empty and proves nothing; and the loss is **not** a whole-origin eviction — a boot was captured with `localStorage` intact (`freshWebMarker: false`, 241 boots) and zero PowerSync databases on disk, recreated 0.7 s later. So don't infer "storage was evicted" from localStorage state, and don't infer "database is fine" from the marker surviving. For **client-written "sticky" state that doesn't replicate back from Postgres** (read-state, dismissals, local prefs), don't trust the synced table alone — ALSO mirror to `localStorage` and merge latest-wins (this caused the "tasks keep resetting to unread" bug; fixed in `apps/web/src/lib/taskReads.ts`).

steps.label: Never compare a SYNCED timestamp with a string in local SQL — read it out and compare instants through `parseSyncedTs`.

lines.t: - **`VITE_DISABLE_AUTH=true` makes every REST-backed page unverifiable locally, and it fails BEFORE the network so nothing appears in devtools.** The flag installs no `ApiTokenContext` provider, so `useApiToken()` falls back to the context default (`() => Promise.resolve(null)`) and `apiFetch` throws `ApiError(401, 'not signed in')` **without issuing a request** (`apps/web/src/lib/api.ts`). The page therefore renders its read-error branch — for /music, «Не вдалося прочитати стан підключення» — which reads exactly like a broken API or a bad Vite proxy, and a request log shows zero `/api/` calls to contradict it. This is fine for the local-first pages (PowerSync serves them) and fatal for the REST ones: **/music, and any other page whose data comes from `apiFetch`**. Measured 2026-08-31 while hiding the music duel behind the Spotify rate limit.

**To drive one anyway, with no docker** (the documented `docker compose up -d` stack was unavailable on that host): boot the REAL API on the test harness's in-process Postgres — `buildHarness()` from `apps/api/test/harness.ts`, seed what the page needs, then `Bun.serve({ port: 3001, fetch: (req) => h.app.fetch(req) })` — since Vite already proxies `/api` → `:3001` and the harness's fake auth defaults to its own `userId` when no `x-test-user` header is present, so an unauthenticated browser request resolves to a real user. Then temporarily wrap the `AUTH_DISABLED` tree in `main.tsx` with `<ApiTokenContext.Provider value={() => Promise.resolve('dev-token')}>` (the harness ignores the token's value) and drive the page with the repo's own puppeteer. **Revert that `main.tsx` edit before committing** — it is a local probe, not a change. And **always run the negative control**: a duel card missing under a throttle and a duel card missing because the seeded pool was empty look identical.

- **A LOCAL-FIRST (PowerSync-backed) page is the opposite case, and it needs no API at all: dev mode already exposes the local database as `window.__jgdb`, so you can seed the exact rows and drive the real page.** The bullet above is about REST pages, where `VITE_DISABLE_AUTH` breaks `apiFetch`; a page that reads its data through `useQuery` has the mirror problem — it renders its empty state, because dev mode uses a separate `juggernaut-dev.db` that never syncs, so there is nothing to look at. `main.tsx` sets `window.__jgdb` on the dev branch (next to `createPowerSyncDb('juggernaut-dev.db')`), and the client schema builds every synced table's view whether or not a row ever arrived — so `await window.__jgdb.execute('INSERT INTO <table> (...) VALUES (?,…)')` from puppeteer, then reload, and the page renders against real-shaped data with no docker, no API and no temporary source edit. Used to verify `/rodovid` at 390 and 1440 (2026-09-03). **Two traps that cost a run each:** a FRESH `--user-data-dir` per launch means a fresh IndexedDB, so the seed from a previous browser is gone — seed inside the same browser session you assert in; and shape the fixture like the PROJECTOR's output rather than what the column names suggest (a Gramps family event carries `{kind:'family', handle:<familyHandle>}`, not the spouses, and a fixture using the wrong shape made a broken filter look correct).

- **Never compare a SYNCED timestamp with a string in local SQL — read it out and compare instants through `parseSyncedTs`.** One row takes two text forms in the client's SQLite: what this device wrote (`toISOString()`, `2026-09-25T21:40:00.000Z`) and what the same row becomes once it round-trips through Postgres (`2026-09-25 21:40:00+00`). At character 10 `' '` sorts before `'T'`, so `WHERE taken_at >= ?` against an ISO bound silently drops every synced row whose UTC date equals the bound's — i.e. exactly the rows just after local midnight. It passes every local test (the fixture rows are the locally written form) and every live check made after the UTC date has rolled. Caught by review on task caf416ed (the pills-day «dose recorded tonight» check), where a 04:09 live run had looked clean. Select the column (`json_group_array` if you need one row) and filter in JS; `lib/synced-time.ts` also covers the Safari/Chrome parse traps.

- **PowerSync upload contract**: jsonb `payload` columns arrive as JSON **strings** (PowerSync stores jsonb as TEXT on the client) — the handler `JSON.parse`s them before Drizzle, and rejects malformed JSON with 400 rather than dropping it. The browser→API call is **cross-origin**, so the API runs `hono/cors` before auth (`WEB_ORIGIN` allowlist); without it the upload preflight 401s and silently never persists.

- **A picked `FileList` is LIVE — copy it with `Array.from` BEFORE clearing the input, never inside a `setState` updater.** The idiom `setFiles((cur) => [...cur, ...Array.from(e.target.files)]); input.value = ''` loses the files whenever React defers the updater, which it does as soon as another update is already queued in the same handler (a `setError(null)` just before is enough): clearing `value` empties the very `FileList` the updater later reads. It works when it is the only update, which is why a one-file click-through passes. Measured 13.09.2026 on the /rodovid materials form (`MaterialIntake`, task 009cb157), caught only by a headless drive that picked two files after an earlier validation error.

- **An OPTIMISTIC HIDE makes CARD-LOCAL error state structurally unable to report its own failure — by the time the write fails, the component that issued it has UNMOUNTED.** The pattern is everywhere in this app: a tap removes the row from the list at once, the POST goes out, and a rejection rolls the hide back. What the rollback mounts is a *fresh* component with fresh state, so a `useState` error living in the card is discarded on precisely the path the error handling exists for — and the result is byte-identical to having no handler at all, which is why it survives review as a finished fix. **Key pending/error state by ROW ID in the list that owns the rows, not in the card.** Measured 12.09.2026 on the vinyl board (`components/vinyl-board.tsx`), where the first version of the swallowed-error fix did exactly this and was caught by the cross-vendor reviewer. Two riders found while fixing it, both worth checking wherever this shape appears: **a rollback callback that ALSO gates a button is passed only to the list that renders that button** — here `onLocalRestore` doubles as the «повернути» condition and so was never given to the active list, leaving the failure branch a silent no-op for over a month; and **an audit that greps for `.catch(() => {})` misses the dangerous sibling** — a catch with a *body* that does a partial recovery (roll back the hide) and no logging is exactly as invisible, and is what `OfferCard` had.

- **Validate constraint-bound columns in the client BEFORE a local-first `db.execute` — the optimistic write is not the safety net, the upload is.** A value that violates a Postgres constraint (a decimal into an `integer` column, an out-of-enum string, a NOT-NULL left null, a value the applier 400s) writes fine to the local SQLite and renders optimistically, then **fails the PowerSync upload and WEDGES the whole upload queue** — every later write stalls behind the poison entry, silently. So the web write path must mirror the server applier's checks (type/range/enum/not-null) before `db.execute`, and a fresh singleton row must seed its NOT-NULL columns. Bit us on books `total_pages`/`current_page` (decimals) and the newborn benefits/config seed (`vitamin_d_enabled`); both caught by codex/pre-empted. This is the client-side twin of the applier validation — a bad value never reaching the queue is the only reliable guard.

- **Every synced table the client WRITES to needs a case in the upload applier — a missing one wedges that device's entire queue, not just that table.** The bullet above is about a bad VALUE; this is the same wedge reached by a table the applier simply doesn't know, which falls through to the default `unsupported table` 400. One batch is one server transaction, so the poison entry takes its innocent batch-mates down with it and PowerSync retries the pair forever. Diagnosed 2026-08-10: deleting a comment that had a file attached uploads `{comment_attachments: 1, task_comments: 1}` (`deleteComment` clears both tables in one local transaction), `comment_attachments` had no applier case, and the phone uploaded **nothing** for the next four hours — 167 identical failures, `applied=0` every time. **The signature is the giveaway, because it looks nothing like a sync bug**: reads keep flowing, the app looks connected, the sync service is green, and the only tell is the client's **write checkpoint frozen at one number while the read checkpoint climbs** (`Updated checkpoint: <read> | write: <frozen>` in the `juggernaut-powersync` Railway logs, one line per client). The audit is mechanical, and **`apps/api/test/powersync-applier-coverage.test.ts` now runs it for you** — it diffs the `case '<table>':` labels in `routes/powersync.ts` against every table `apps/web/src`/`apps/mobile/src` runs an INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on, in both directions, so a new synced table that the client writes and the applier doesn't know fails the suite instead of the phone. Its ONE exemption is `apps/mobile/src/visualTest.ts` (build-flag-gated, separate DB); if you add another, prove it cannot reach a real upload queue. Where the client's write is a mirror of an authoritative REST call, the applier case should **acknowledge and do nothing** rather than repeat the mutation: a second destructive path keyed only on a row id is what a replayed queue entry turns into a data-loss bug. **The wedge is now also VISIBLE**: `apps/web/src/powersync/uploadQueueHealth.ts` counts consecutive upload failures and watches the pending queue, and `UploadQueueAlert` in `components/shell-shared.tsx` puts a red strip under the header of both shells (plus a fourth `SyncStatusPill` state) — the pill's other three states are all download signals, which is why it read СИНХРОНІЗОВАНО throughout the four-hour outage.

- **`ON CONFLICT` ARBITRATES ONE INDEX, so retargeting an upsert from `id` to a natural key leaves the PRIMARY KEY uncovered — and `entry.id` is client-supplied.** The applier's tables are almost all `target: <table>.id`, which quietly handles any duplicate id; the moment you switch to a natural key (`pill_intakes`, `nanny_week_override`, `silpo_product_link`) a PUT whose id already belongs to a DIFFERENT row raises 23505 instead, and one batch is one transaction, so that is the same whole-device wedge as the bullet above — re-entered by the door you just opened. Two distinct cases, and the same-user one needs no attacker: a client reusing an id it already spent on another day names a `(pill, date)` that does not exist, so the arbiter never fires. Fix it in two caller-scoped layers, never with a cross-user lookup (that is a `User scoping` violation, and it also leaks a cross-account existence oracle through whether the stored id came back unchanged — both were caught by `codex review` on 2026-09-07, task 22209dd3): resolve the caller's OWN row under that id and mint a fresh one if its natural key differs, then wrap the insert in a **SAVEPOINT** (`tx.transaction`) and treat a surviving 23505 as "the id belongs to a row I may not see" — retry under a fresh uuid. `applyPillIntakesEntry` and the `media_duel` daily-slot upsert are the two worked examples; the id is an internal handle, so replacing it costs nothing next to failing the upload. ⚠️ A SELECT alone is not enough — it is a TOCTOU race, which is exactly what the savepoint is for.

- **A column on a `SELECT *` synced table cannot be shipped by an UNATTENDED run — the precondition is unverifiable at night, so design around it instead of waiting.** The bullet below makes the client schema declare a new column before the migration adds it; the note on `pills.profile_id` adds that the declaration must also have reached the PHONE via a Capgo OTA first, because `apps/mobile` bundles the same schema file and cannot learn it from a git push. **What nobody wrote down is that a night run cannot CHECK that.** The only signal for which bundle the phone holds is the `build_info` row it logs at boot, and BetterStack's SQL-queryable retention is **~1 hour** (measured 2026-09-01: `min(dt)` 02:50Z, `max(dt)` 03:50Z) — so a phone that has not been woken inside that hour simply cannot be asked, and no amount of waiting helps at 04:00. The honest options are therefore two, and "apply it anyway" is not one: split the increment across two runs the way `pills.profile_id` was, or **pick a shape that touches no synced table at all**. Increment 5 of the medical miniapp took the second: its provenance ledger `medical_extraction` (migration 0141) is server-only — absent from the sync rules, the publication and the client schema, the same treatment as `medical_visit_document_blob` — which invalidates no bucket, needs no OTA, and shipped in one run. Reach for that whenever the new data has no client reader yet.

- **On an audit/provenance table pointing INTO client-written tables, a foreign key is a trap in BOTH directions — use a plain uuid.** `ON DELETE CASCADE` looks like the tidy choice and silently destroys the very thing the table exists for: deleting a source document took its provenance rows with it while the medications and readings they explained survived, i.e. machine-written rows that had become indistinguishable from hand-typed ones. `ON DELETE RESTRICT` is worse — it is evaluated **inside the PowerSync upload transaction**, so a client deleting a parent row turns into a poisoned batch and freezes that device's entire upload queue (the wedge two bullets up). Both were caught in review on `medical_extraction`, which now carries no FK at all on `document_id`, `pill_id` or `newborn_event_id` — matching `pill_intakes.pill_id` and `medical_visit.profile_id`, and keeping rollback working after the source is deleted. The general rule: **anything the applier can delete must not be the target of a constraint that can fail.**

- **Three schemas stay in lockstep — adding a column to a synced table is a 3-file change.** A PowerSync-synced table is defined in THREE places that must agree: the Drizzle table (`packages/db-schema/`), the prod Postgres (a migration), and the **web client schema** (`apps/web/src/powersync/schema.ts`). The sync rules `SELECT *` every synced table, so **a column added to the DB but missing from the client schema wedges an already-synced client's incremental sync** — the whole board silently freezes (task state, comments, sessions stop updating on the UI even though writes persist server-side; a _fresh_ client looks fine, which makes it easy to miss). This bit us once (`recurrence_assignee_id` on task_recurrence). When you add/rename/drop a column on a synced table, update all three. `apps/api/test/powersync-schema-sync.test.ts` enforces it — it parses the sync rules + Drizzle columns + the web schema and fails if a `SELECT *` table's client schema is missing a column. **Explicit-column tables have a fourth contract:** every column used by the sync rule, including an owner used only in `WHERE`, must also be in the Postgres publication projection. `comment_attachments` omitted `user_id` there and silently vanished from every by_user bucket while REST kept working (fixed by 0093; guarded by the same test). Its curated client projection may still omit server-only columns. **A whole NEW synced table is another publication step**: prod uses an explicit table list (not `FOR ALL TABLES`), so add it via an `ALTER PUBLICATION` migration, and row-touch anything written before membership or projection was correct — full pattern + symptoms in the repo `railway` skill. **And warn the user BEFORE you ship it: any sync-rules change invalidates every bucket, so every client re-downloads its ENTIRE bucket once** (`reason="checkpoint_superseded"`). Measured 2026-08-12 adding `media_duel`: the phone pulled **38 335 operations / 51 MB over ~7 minutes**, during which the sync pill honestly showed the LAST COMPLETED sync — a timestamp frozen ~30 min in the past — and read exactly like a sync outage. Nothing is broken and it self-heals; the cost is the surprise. Say it in the report, and expect a stale pill for minutes after any sync-rules deploy.

- **Clearing a field on a recurrence BLUEPRINT is not done until every OCCURRENCE row is cleared too — otherwise the next schedule edit silently puts it back.** `applyRecurrenceUpload` (`apps/api/src/routes/powersync.ts`) computes `recValues.brief = hasBrief ? resolved.brief : (existingRecurrence?.brief ?? null)` — and the same line for `skill` — then feeds that straight into `blueprintSet`. A PATCH carries only the columns that changed, so **any ordinary schedule edit in the web UI reads the OCCURRENCE's stored value and writes it back onto the blueprint**. Measured 2026-08-26 while emptying the `brief` column: 103 `task_recurrence` rows still held text, and three of those texts belonged to blueprints that migrations `0119`/`0120` had cleaned weeks earlier — all of them one schedule tap away from resurrection. So a data migration that nulls a blueprint field must null the mirrors in the same transaction (0117, 0119, 0120, 0122 and 0128 all do), and a cleanup that touches only `task_recurrence_blueprints` is not a smaller version of the change — it is a change that undoes itself. The trap outlives `brief`: `skill` travels the identical path.

- **`money_transactions`' `amount` is in the OPERATION currency, `balanceAfter` in the ACCOUNT's — never do arithmetic across the two without checking `currencyCode`.** The MCP tool says so, and it is still easy to miss because both render as plain numbers. Cost a wrong published diagnosis on 2026-08-19: the ФОП account's incoming leg reads `amount: 1575, currencyCode: 978, balanceAfter: 81112.5` — 1575 **EUR**, 81 112.50 **UAH** — and reasoning `81112.5 - 1575` produced a confident, wrong chain. The raw `money_monobank_transaction.amount` column IS in account currency (there: `+8_111_250` kopiykas), which is why the code was right while the human-facing explanation was not. **When a row's `currencyCode` differs from its account's currency, the only figure you may combine with `balance` is the raw column, never the tool's `amount`.**

- **A Monobank row's RAW `amount` and RAW `currencyCode` can name DIFFERENT currencies, and on a cross-currency operation they do — so `convertToUah(tx.amount, tx.currencyCode, rates)` over a Monobank row is only correct while the two happen to agree.** The bullet above records that `money_monobank_transaction.amount` is in the **account's** currency; the other half is that `money_monobank_transaction.currencyCode` is the **operation's**. Both legs of the 2026-08-19 ФОП payout show it: the ФОП **euro** account's leg is `amount −157_500` (−1 575.00 **EUR**, the account) with `currencyCode 980` (**UAH**, the operation), and the ФОП **hryvnia** account's leg is `amount +8_111_250` (81 112.50 **UAH**) with `currencyCode 978` (**EUR**). Because a same-currency operation is the overwhelming normal case, anything built on "currencyCode describes amount" looks correct for months and then silently mis-scales one row by the FX rate. `income-rollup.ts` did exactly this pairing until 2026-08-28 and now resolves the account's currency through `MonobankAccountInfo.currencyCode`; the trap itself is live for any NEW code, so resolve the ACCOUNT's currency through `accountId` in `moneyAccount` whenever the two may differ. ⚠️ And note `money_account.currency` is a **text** column that may hold `'EUR'` as easily as `'978'` — a bare `Number()` yields NaN, which compares equal to nothing (so a same-currency pair reads as cross-currency) and matches no rate series, so the failure is a silently dropped figure rather than an error. Use `toCurrencyCode`.

- **A transfer's two legs are valued at the transfer day's own NBU rate, and their hryvnia difference is a FEE — never income.** Shipped 2026-08-28 (`633d229`) to Yarik's rule: negative difference → an expense in `finance`, positive → a return that subtracts from it. The one implementation is `computeTransferFeeUah` (`miniapps/money/src/transfer-fx.ts`); the spend rollup books it for Monobank **and** manual pairs, and `withVirtualTransferFees` emits the matching ledger row, so the bar and its drilldown agree. Two rules inside it are load-bearing and were each proven by deleting them: a CROSS-currency pair with no same-day rate returns **null and books nothing** (its delta is what survives subtracting two large converted numbers, so any other day's rate is noise the size of the answer), while a SAME-currency delta may fall back to today's rates (a few units of one currency, which an off-day rate can only mis-scale slightly). The day key is **Kyiv, not UTC** — the 19.08.2026 payout is 21:08Z on the 18th, and the wrong day moves a 520 ₴ answer by 35 ₴. What this replaced: the Monobank branch subtracted the legs' RAW amounts without comparing currencies and booked any positive result as «Курсова різниця» income, which on that payout was `81 112,50 ₴ − 1 575,00 € = 79 537,50` — 18% of August 2026's reported income, from money that was never income. **August now reads 371 213,63 ₴ against 450 755 ₴ before, verified on prod.** ⚠️ **These conversions are ROUTINE, not a one-off**: the 2026-08-25 session concluded from a description-text search that the 19.08 transfer was the only one in the history, and the shipped rollup immediately found spreads in June, July and August (−592,12 ₴ in August alone). Searching descriptions is not how you find them — pair detection is.

- **Income figures come from the ROLLUP, never from `/api/money/transactions` — the two disagree three ways, and the transactions endpoint is the wrong source for anything that must tie out to the income bars.** `GET /api/money/income` already returns each bucket's own rows as `byCategory[].transactions[]` (`IncomeTxSummary` — id/description/amount/timestamp, newest-first, `miniapps/money/src/income-rollup.ts`), so per-transaction income detail needs **no second fetch**; the field was on the wire and merely untyped in the web client until 2026-08-23. Reach for `/api/money/transactions` instead and the page contradicts itself, because that endpoint (a) reports **raw operation currency** while the rollup stores `amountUah` — Aug-2026 deposit interest is `20.78 USD` there and ~831 ₴ in the bar; (b) derives its **own category** (refunds become `return`, transfers `finance`, and the 21.08 «Універсал Банк» row read `pension` against a Пенсія bar of 4 225 ₴); and (c) applies **`limit` before any direction filter**, and income is ~3% of the ledger (9 of 327 rows in 2026-08, with five of six sampled months hitting the 500-row cap), so a client-side `isIncome` filter silently truncates. It also cannot see rows the INCOME rollup synthesizes; note the transfer FX line is no longer one of them — since 2026-08-28 it is a fee, and `/api/money/transactions` is now precisely where it does appear. Verified on prod across four months: summing `byCategory[].transactions[]` equals `totalIncome` to the cent, and every bucket's rows sum to its own `totalAmount`.

- **Monobank stamps a transfer's two legs to the SAME second, so "the latest transaction" is never `ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 1`.** On a tie Postgres returns an arbitrary row, and for a running-balance read that is a coin flip between the transfer's intermediate and final state. Shipped as a wrong balance: a ФОП account emptied on 2026-08-18 carried two rows both at 21:08:04Z (`+1 575 → 81 112.50`, then `−81 112.50 → 0`) and the app showed 81 113 грн — in the account card AND in the daily net-worth snapshot, which read the same way. The order is recoverable without the timestamps, because a row's OPENING balance is `balance - amount` and the last row's closing balance opens nothing; `latestAccountBalance` (`miniapps/money/src/latest-account-balance.ts`) does that reconstruction and is the ONLY way to read a Monobank account's current balance — use it rather than re-deriving. It returns `no_transactions` / `indeterminate` rather than guessing, and callers keep their previous value; two rules pull opposite ways and are applied at different points, so keep them straight when editing: the scan cap is judged on the RAW row count (dedupe would hide an overflow) while the chain runs on the DEDUPED list (the plun import's twins share ts+amount+balance and would otherwise read as two rival terminal rows and freeze the balance). Read the tied group with `gte(ts, max)`, never `eq` — the driver millisecond-truncates the Date, so `eq` against a finer-precision `ts` matches nothing and freezes the balance silently. **Still open:** `/accounts/balance-history` has no tie-break, so the account page's 180-day chart can still order a tied group arbitrarily.

- **A manual money row's INCOME category is `raw.incomeCategoryId || category_id`, not the column alone.** That is the precedence `income-rollup.ts` uses, and any new income reader must match it — including the `||` rather than `??`: `raw` is unvalidated jsonb, so an empty string is storable, and `??` would let it shadow a valid column value while the rollup fell through and counted the row. ⚠️ This is the INCOME half only — manual **expenses** deliberately keep their category in the column (`set-category.ts` writes it there and refuses every non-expense row), and the combined-ledger reader branches by transaction kind. Two existing readers use `??` rather than `||` (`recent-transactions.ts`, and the ICU coupon path in `apps/web/src/routes/money.tsx`); they differ only on an empty-string `raw` value, so this is a divergence to know about rather than a live bug. `addIncome` does write the column, so it is often right; imported, recategorised and coupon rows may carry the authoritative value in `raw` (the coupon job writes both), and a «Коригування балансу» row can read `category_id: 'budget_correction'` with the real category in `raw`. Reading the column alone is a SILENT undercount, not an error — measured 2026-09-05, when the deposits model shipped to prod understating two deposits' earned interest because every local fixture was hand-built with the field already populated (see the database-boundary rule in `development-process`).

- **An unrecognised currency resolves to the HRYVNIA CODE, so a guard written against the code is not a guard — ask whether the currency is CONVERTIBLE, not whether it is foreign.** `money_account.currency` is unconstrained text, and `normalizeDepositCurrency` (`miniapps/money/src/deposit-portfolio.ts`) returns `CURRENCY_CODES[alpha] ?? UAH_CODE` — so a `CAD` row arrives carrying `code: 980` with `alpha: 'CAD'`, sails past the natural `if (!rates && code !== UAH_CODE) withhold`, and `convertToUah` then returns it untouched: **1 000 CAD published as 1 000 ₴, silently.** The same shape is available to any new hryvnia total, because the normalizer is doing exactly what its name promises and the wrongness lives in the caller's test. Ask `CURRENCY_CODES[alpha] !== undefined` (`isConvertibleCurrency`) instead, and withhold the WHOLE figure rather than dropping the member — dropping is the silent understatement the all-or-nothing rule exists to prevent. Caught by `codex review` on 2026-09-06 while the deposits page was gaining its hryvnia row; the bug predated that change. ⚠️ Note the two guards are not interchangeable: a missing RATE is a transient condition that a hryvnia-only member can be exempt from, while an unconvertible CURRENCY can never be converted at any rate, so it withholds whether or not rates arrived.
